Hoe ongelooflik is dit dat God ’n ellendige sondaar, sonder enige vrees vir die Here, kan neem en hom in ’n bloedgewaste heilige en verkondiger van die evangelie kan verander! In hierdie verhaal sien ons God se lewensveranderende krag aan die werk in die lewe van ons gesangeskrywer.

In die klein begraafplaas op ’n kerkterrein in Olney, Engeland, staan ’n granietgrafsteen met hierdie inskripsie, wat Newton self voor sy dood geskryf het:

John Newton, eens ’n ongelowige en losbandige man, ’n dienaar van slawe in Afrika, is deur die ryke barmhartigheid van ons Here en Verlosser Jesus Christus bewaar, herstel, vergewe en aangestel om die geloof te verkondig wat hy lank probeer vernietig het!

Hierdie grafskrif beskryf op gepaste wyse die ongewone en kleurryke lewe van hierdie man, een van die groot evangeliese predikers van die agtiende eeu. Sy getuienis was: “Deur die genade van God is ek wat ek is!”

“Wonderbare genade” is ’n gesang wat in 1779 gepubliseer is, met woorde wat in 1772 deur die Engelse digter en Anglikaanse geestelike John Newton (1725–1807) geskryf is. “Wonderbare genade” is waarskynlik die mees geliefde gesang van die afgelope twee eeue. Daar word geraam dat hierdie gesang jaarliks 10 miljoen keer uitgevoer word. Dit het op meer as 11 000 albums verskyn en is in ongeveer 60 tale vertaal. Daar is daarna verwys in Harriet Beecher Stowe se roman teen slawerny, Uncle Tom’s Cabin. Dit het gedurende twee van Amerika se grootste krisisse baie gewild geword: die Burgeroorlog en die Viëtnamoorlog.

Ironies genoeg is hierdie aangrypende lied, wat nou met die Afro-Amerikaanse gemeenskap verbind word, deur ’n voormalige slawehandelaar, John Newton, geskryf.

John is op 24 Julie 1725 in Wapping, Engeland, gebore as die seun van ’n seevarende vader, John Newton, Sr., en ’n toegewyde Christenmoeder, Elizabeth Newton. Sy vader het hom liefgehad, maar was die meeste van die tyd op see. Sy moeder daarenteen was teer en versorgend en het hom die Woord van God geleer. Sy het hom geleer om die Bybel hele hoofstukke op ’n slag te memoriseer en hom kerk toe geneem. Ongelukkig is sy moeder aan tuberkulose oorlede toe hy byna sewe was. Sy vader het kort daarna weer getrou en hom na ’n kosskool gestuur. Gedurende sy tyd op kosskool het hy slegte vriende gemaak. Sy karakter het so agteruitgegaan dat hy uit een skool ontslaan en na ’n ander verskuif is. Teen die tyd dat hy 11 jaar oud was, wou die kosskole hom nie meer hê nie, en sy vader het hom dus saam see toe geneem. Hy het die volgende ses jaar saam met sy vader op die Atlantiese Oseaan deurgebring.

Toe John 17 was, het sy vader gereël om hom na Jamaika te stuur vir ’n goed betaalde werk as opsigter op ’n plantasie. Op pad daarheen, terwyl hy gewag het dat die skip vertrek, het John ’n uitnodiging ontvang om die huis van ou vriende, die Catletts, te besoek. Dit was in hierdie huis dat John se moeder tien jaar tevore gesterf het. Terwyl hy weer met hulle kennis gemaak het, het hy hul dogter, Mary, leer ken. John en Mary se moeders was die beste vriende. John is genooi om vier dae te bly, maar hy het twee weke gebly en die skip na Jamaika gemis.

Op 18-jarige ouderdom is John vir diens in die Koninklike Vloot opgeroep, en sy lewe het van kwaad na erger gegaan. Hy wou terugkeer om Mary te sien, en het dus van die skip gedros, maar is gevang, in die openbaar gegesel en in boeie geslaan. Sy lewe op die skip was so goddeloos dat selfs die ander goddelose matrose teruggedeins het vir sy gevloek en laster. Hy het die bynaam “Die Groot Godslasteraar” gekry en was so onwelkom op die skip dat hy gestuur is om op ’n slaweskip te werk.

Een van die eienaars van die slaweskip waarop hy nou gewerk het, het John ’n werk aangebied sodra hulle die kus van Afrika bereik het. Toe hy egter aan wal was, is hy vasgebind en gedwing om te werk met min kos, klere of skuiling. Hy het gedurende hierdie tyd verskeie briewe aan sy vader gestuur waarin hy om hulp gesmeek het.

’n Skip genaamd The Greyhound het naby die kus gevaar wat John nou sy tuiste genoem het. John se vader het die kaptein opdrag gegee om na sy seun te soek. Hoewel die skip byna te ver van die kus af was om handel te dryf, het hulle besluit om dit te probeer. ’n Vriend van John het van die kus af na die skip geroei om handel te dryf. Toe hy omdraai om te vertrek, het die kaptein hom gevra of hy iemand met die naam John Newton ken. Tot die kaptein se verbasing het hy hom wel geken, en John is aan boord gebring om huis toe te gaan.

Aan boord van die skip het Newton ’n eksemplaar van Thomas á Kempis se Christelike klassieke werk, The Imitation of Christ, opgetel. Hy het nog nooit iets soortgelyks teëgekom nie en het begin wonder of die Christelike aansprake dalk waar kon wees. Daardie nag, op 10 Maart 1748, het ’n hewige storm die skip byna laat sink. Mans, diere en voorrade is oorboord gespoel. Die storm het Newton wakker gemaak; die golwe het die skip se verrotte houtwerk gebreek en vloedwater het sy kajuit binnegestroom. John het vir die eerste keer in jare gebid.

The Greyhound is meer as 11 dae lank in die Noord-Atlantiese storm rondgeslinger. Met min hoop op oorlewing het die matrose werktuiglik die pompe bedien in ’n poging om die vaartuig bo water te hou. Op die elfde dag van die storm was John te uitgeput om te pomp, en is hy dus aan die roer vasgebind, waar hy sy bes gedoen het om die skip op koers te hou. Van eenuur tot middernag was hy aan die roer. Hy was bang dat hy sou sterf, en as die Christelike geloof waar was, sou hy sekerlik nie vergewe word nie. Hy het nagedink oor alles wat hy die afgelope paar jaar gedoen het. Sy lewe het net so verwoes en stukkend gelyk soos die gehawende skip wat hy deur die storm probeer stuur het. Gedurende daardie lang en uitputtende ure het Newton tot God uitgeroep soos nog nooit tevore nie, en dit was die keerpunt in sy lewe.

Dit was ’n dag wat John Newton vir altyd onthou het. “Op daardie dag het die Here van omhoog gestuur en my uit diep waters gered.” Meer as 50 jaar later het John op 21 Maart 1805 in sy dagboek geskryf: “Nie goed in staat om te skryf nie; maar ek probeer om die terugkeer van hierdie dag met verootmoediging, gebed en lof te herdenk.”

Slegs God se wonderbare genade kon ’n onbeskofte, goddelose matroos wat slawehandel gedryf het, neem en hom in ’n kind van God verander. John het nooit opgehou om verwonderd te staan oor God se werk in sy lewe nie. Hy het belangstelling begin toon in gebed, die lees en oordenking van die Skrif, en daarin om slegs woorde te spreek wat God behaag.

Toe hy huis toe terugkeer, het Mary en haar ouers die verandering raakgesien wat die Here in John teweeggebring het. Die twee is op 1 Februarie 1750 getroud.

Vir die volgende vier jaar was Newton kaptein van sy eie slaweskip. Hierdie beroep het hom maande op ’n slag van Mary geskei gehou. Terwyl hulle uitmekaar was, het die twee voortdurend gekorrespondeer. In sy briewe het John herhaaldelik geskryf hoe hul liefde en huwelik sy dankbaarheid en erkentlikheid teenoor die Here laat toeneem het. “... Wanneer ek myself toelaat om in besonder aan jou te dink, voer dit my gewoonlik verder en bring dit my op my knieë om die Here te loof omdat Hy my so ’n skat gegee het, en om vir jou vrede en welsyn te bid”

John het probeer om sy slaweskip te “verchristelik” deur Sondagdienste vir sy bemanning van 30 manne wat deur die sonde verhard was, te hou. Hy het nog drie reise onderneem om slawe van Afrika na Noord-Amerika te bring. Terwyl hy sy vierde reis beplan het, het hy malaria opgedoen. God het hierdie siekte gebruik om sy betrokkenheid by die slawehandel te beëindig.

Toe John ’n nuwe hoofstuk in sy lewe begin het, het hy hom geroepe gevoel om ’n predikant te word. Hy het meer as 50 jaar lank die evangelie verkondig en was een van die invloedrykste manne van sy tyd.

John Newton het dikwels ’n gesang geskryf wat by sy Sondagaanddienste gepas het. In 1779 is 280 hiervan versamel en saamgevoeg met 68 gesange deur Newton se vriend en gemeentelid, William Cowper, en as die Olney Hymns gepubliseer. Die bekendste van al die Olney Hymns, “Die geloof se terugblik en verwagting”, het voortgevloei uit Dawid se uitroep in 1 Kronieke 17:16-17. Ons ken dit vandag as “Wonderbare genade”. “Wonderbare genade” het oorspronklik ses strofes gehad, en die laaste strofe is ongeveer ’n eeu later bygevoeg. Die meeste gesangboeke bevat vier of vyf van hierdie strofes.

As predikant in die kerk het John al hoe meer besorgd geraak oor die slawehandel wat steeds voortgeduur het. In 1788, 34 jaar nadat hy die slawehandel verlaat het, het hy ’n boek getiteld Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade geskryf en dit aan al die parlementslede gestuur. Hierdie boek het die publiek bewus gemaak van die euwels van die slawehandel. Hy haal die volgende aan: “Dit spreek vanself dat die vang, verkoop en vervoer van swart slawe na die plantasies in die Wes-Indiese Eilande en Amerika ’n wrede en bose lewenswyse was.” Met God se hulp en voorsienigheid het John in 1807, etlike maande voor sy dood, die dag beleef toe slawerny amptelik in Engeland verbied is.

Toe John in sy sestigerjare was, is sy geliefde vrou Mary oorlede. Dit was ’n groot beproewing vir John, en hy het die oorblywende 17 jaar van sy lewe sonder haar deurgebring.

Nadat John ’n beroerte gehad het en kort voor sy dood, het ’n woordvoerder van die kerk Newton aangemoedig om dit te oorweeg om weens sy verswakkende gesondheid, sig en geheue op te hou preek. John het geantwoord: “Wat, moet die ou godslasteraar uit Afrika ophou terwyl hy nog kan praat? Ek sal aanhou preek. Hoewel my geheue verswak, onthou ek twee dinge baie duidelik: ek is ’n groot sondaar, en Christus is ’n groot Verlosser.”

Die laaste woorde van John Newton terwyl hy op sy sterfbed gelê het, was soos volg: “Ek is nog in die land van die sterwendes; ek sal binnekort in die land van die lewendes wees.”

Die melodie van “Wonderbare genade” is ’n vroeë Amerikaanse volksmelodie. Dit was aanvanklik bekend as ’n plantasiemelodie getiteld “Liefdevolle lammers”. Hierdie melodie is die eerste keer in 1831 in die boek The Virginia Harmony gepubliseer. Die meeste gesangboeke wat ná hierdie tyd gepubliseer is, het hierdie lied ingesluit. In 1910 het Edwin O. Excell die laaste strofe bygevoeg, wat uiteindelik die laaste drie oorspronklike strofes van die lied vervang het. Sy weergawe van die lied kom vandag die algemeenste in ons gesangboeke voor. Verskeie ander Olney-gesange deur Newton word vandag steeds gesing, waaronder “Hoe soet klink die Naam van Jesus” en “Heerlike dinge word van U gesê”.

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Wie unglaublich ist es doch, dass Gott einen elenden Sünder, dem jede Furcht des Herrn fehlt, zu einem durch das Blut gereinigten Heiligen und Prediger des Evangeliums machen kann! In dieser Geschichte sehen wir Gottes lebensverändernde Kraft im Leben unseres Liederdichters am Werk.

Auf dem kleinen Kirchhof in Olney, England, steht ein Grabstein aus Granit mit dieser Inschrift, die Newton selbst vor seinem Tod verfasste:

John Newton, einst ein Ungläubiger und Wüstling, ein Diener von Sklaven in Afrika, wurde durch die reiche Barmherzigkeit unseres Herrn und Erlösers Jesus Christus bewahrt, wiederhergestellt, begnadigt und dazu berufen, den Glauben zu predigen, den er lange mit aller Kraft zu zerstören versucht hatte!

Diese Grabinschrift beschreibt treffend das ungewöhnliche und bewegte Leben dieses Mannes, eines der großen evangelischen Prediger des achtzehnten Jahrhunderts. Sein Zeugnis lautete: „Durch Gottes Gnade bin ich, was ich bin!“

„Amazing Grace“ ist ein Kirchenlied, das 1779 veröffentlicht wurde und dessen Text der englische Dichter und anglikanische Geistliche John Newton (1725–1807) im Jahr 1772 verfasste. „Amazing Grace“ ist wahrscheinlich das beliebteste Kirchenlied der letzten zwei Jahrhunderte. Schätzungen zufolge wird dieses Lied jährlich 10 Millionen Mal aufgeführt. Es ist auf über 11.000 Alben erschienen und in etwa 60 Sprachen übersetzt worden. In Harriet Beecher Stowes gegen die Sklaverei gerichtetem Roman Onkel Toms Hütte wurde darauf Bezug genommen. Während zweier der größten Krisen Amerikas – des Bürgerkriegs und des Vietnamkriegs – nahm seine Beliebtheit stark zu.

Ironischerweise wurde dieses bewegende Lied, das eng mit der afroamerikanischen Gemeinschaft verbunden ist, von einem ehemaligen Sklavenhändler geschrieben: John Newton.

John wurde am 24. Juli 1725 in Wapping, England, geboren. Sein Vater, John Newton sen., war Seefahrer, seine Mutter, Elizabeth Newton, eine fromme Christin. Sein Vater liebte ihn, war aber die meiste Zeit auf See. Seine Mutter hingegen war liebevoll und fürsorglich und lehrte ihn das Wort Gottes. Sie leitete ihn dazu an, ganze Kapitel der Bibel auswendig zu lernen, und nahm ihn mit zur Kirche. Leider starb seine Mutter an Tuberkulose, als er fast sieben Jahre alt war. Sein Vater heiratete kurze Zeit später erneut und schickte ihn auf ein Internat. Während seiner Zeit dort geriet er an schlechte Freunde. Sein Charakter verschlechterte sich so sehr, dass er von einer Schule verwiesen wurde und auf eine andere wechselte. Als er elf Jahre alt war, wollten die Internate ihn nicht mehr aufnehmen, und so nahm ihn sein Vater mit auf See. Die nächsten sechs Jahre verbrachte er mit seinem Vater auf dem Atlantik.

Als John 17 Jahre alt war, sorgte sein Vater dafür, dass er nach Jamaika geschickt werden sollte, um dort eine gut bezahlte Stelle als Aufseher einer Plantage anzutreten. Auf dem Weg dorthin erhielt John, während er auf die Abfahrt des Schiffes wartete, eine Einladung in das Haus alter Freunde, der Familie Catlett. In diesem Haus war Johns Mutter zehn Jahre zuvor gestorben. Als er den Kontakt zu ihnen wieder aufnahm, lernte er ihre Tochter Mary kennen. Johns und Marys Mütter waren die besten Freundinnen gewesen. John war eingeladen worden, vier Tage zu bleiben, doch er blieb zwei Wochen und verpasste das Schiff nach Jamaika.

Mit 18 Jahren wurde John in die Royal Navy eingezogen, und sein Leben wurde immer schlimmer. Er wollte zurückkehren und Mary sehen, deshalb desertierte er vom Schiff, wurde jedoch gefasst, öffentlich ausgepeitscht und in Ketten gelegt. Sein Leben an Bord war so gottlos, dass selbst die anderen gottlosen Seeleute vor seinen Flüchen und Gotteslästerungen zurückschreckten. Er erhielt den Beinamen „Der große Gotteslästerer“ und war an Bord so unerwünscht, dass man ihn zur Arbeit auf ein Sklavenschiff schickte.

Einer der Eigentümer des Sklavenschiffes, auf dem er nun arbeitete, bot John eine Stelle an, sobald sie die afrikanische Küste erreicht hätten. Doch kaum war er an Land, wurde er gefesselt und zur Arbeit gezwungen, wobei er nur wenig Nahrung, Kleidung oder Unterkunft erhielt. In dieser Zeit schickte er mehrere Briefe an seinen Vater und flehte ihn um Hilfe an.

Ein Schiff namens The Greyhound segelte nahe der Küste, die John inzwischen seine Heimat nannte. Der Kapitän war von Johns Vater beauftragt worden, nach seinem Sohn zu suchen. Obwohl das Schiff fast zu weit von der Küste entfernt war, um Handel zu treiben, beschloss man, es dennoch zu versuchen. Ein Freund Johns ruderte vom Ufer hinaus, um Handel zu treiben. Als er sich zum Aufbruch wandte, fragte ihn der Kapitän, ob er jemanden namens John Newton kenne. Zur Überraschung des Kapitäns kannte er ihn tatsächlich, und John wurde an Bord gebracht, um nach Hause zu fahren.

An Bord nahm Newton den christlichen Klassiker Die Nachfolge Christi von Thomas von Kempen zur Hand. Er war noch nie etwas Vergleichbarem begegnet und begann sich zu fragen, ob die Aussagen des christlichen Glaubens wahr sein könnten. In jener Nacht, am 10. März 1748, brachte ein heftiger Sturm das Schiff beinahe zum Sinken. Männer, Tiere und Vorräte wurden über Bord gespült. Der Sturm weckte Newton; die Wellen hatten die morschen Planken des Schiffes zerbrochen, und hereinströmendes Wasser wirbelte in seine Kajüte. John betete zum ersten Mal seit Jahren.

The Greyhound wurde über elf Tage lang im Sturm auf dem Nordatlantik hin und her geworfen. Mit wenig Hoffnung, am Leben zu bleiben, bedienten die Seeleute mechanisch die Pumpen und versuchten, das Schiff über Wasser zu halten. Am elften Tag des Sturms war John zu erschöpft, um zu pumpen. Daher wurde er am Steuer festgebunden, wo er sein Bestes tat, um das Schiff auf Kurs zu halten. Von ein Uhr bis Mitternacht stand er am Steuer. Er fürchtete, sterben zu müssen, und wenn der christliche Glaube wahr wäre, würde ihm gewiss nicht vergeben werden. Er dachte über alles nach, was er in den vergangenen Jahren getan hatte. Sein Leben schien ebenso ruiniert und zerschlagen wie das beschädigte Schiff, das er durch den Sturm zu steuern versuchte. Während dieser langen und zermürbenden Stunden schrie Newton zu Gott wie nie zuvor, und das war der Wendepunkt in seinem Leben.

Dieser Tag blieb John Newton für immer im Gedächtnis. „An diesem Tag sandte der Herr Hilfe aus der Höhe und rettete mich aus tiefen Wassern.“ Über 50 Jahre später schrieb John am 21. März 1805 in sein Tagebuch: „Ich kann kaum schreiben; doch ich bemühe mich, die Wiederkehr dieses Tages mit Demütigung, Gebet und Lobpreis zu begehen.“

Nur Gottes wunderbare Gnade konnte einen rohen, gottlosen, mit Sklaven handelnden Seemann zu einem Kind Gottes machen. John hörte nie auf, voller Ehrfurcht über Gottes Wirken in seinem Leben zu staunen. Er fand Freude am Gebet, am Lesen und Nachsinnen über die Heilige Schrift und daran, nur Worte zu sprechen, die Gott wohlgefällig waren.

Als er nach Hause zurückkehrte, erkannten Mary und ihre Eltern die Veränderung, die der Herr in John bewirkt hatte. Die beiden heirateten am 1. Februar 1750.

In den folgenden vier Jahren war Newton Kapitän seines eigenen Sklavenschiffes. Diese Tätigkeit hielt ihn jeweils monatelang von Mary getrennt. Während ihrer Trennung schrieben die beiden einander ständig. In seinen Briefen schrieb John wiederholt, wie ihre Liebe und Ehe seine Dankbarkeit gegenüber dem Herrn vermehrten. „... Wenn ich mir gönne, ganz besonders an dich zu denken, führt mich das gewöhnlich noch weiter und bringt mich auf die Knie, um den Herrn dafür zu preisen, dass er mir einen solchen Schatz geschenkt hat, und um für deinen Frieden und dein Wohlergehen zu beten.“

John bemühte sich, sein Sklavenschiff zu „christianisieren“, indem er für seine Mannschaft aus 30 in der Sünde verhärteten Männern Sonntagsgottesdienste hielt. Er unternahm noch drei Reisen, um Sklaven aus Afrika nach Nordamerika zu bringen. Als er seine vierte Reise plante, erkrankte er an Malaria. Gott gebrauchte diese Krankheit, um seine Beteiligung am Sklavenhandel zu beenden.

Als John einen neuen Abschnitt seines Lebens begann, fühlte er sich zum geistlichen Dienst berufen. Über 50 Jahre lang predigte er das Evangelium und war einer der einflussreichsten Männer seiner Zeit.

John Newton dichtete oft ein Lied passend zu seinen Sonntagabendgottesdiensten. Im Jahr 1779 wurden 280 dieser Lieder gesammelt, mit 68 Liedern von Newtons Freund und Gemeindeglied William Cowper zusammengeführt und als Olney Hymns veröffentlicht. Das berühmteste aller Lieder der Olney Hymns, „Rückblick und Erwartung des Glaubens“, entstand aus Davids Ausruf in 1. Chronik 17:16-17. Heute kennen wir es als „Amazing Grace“. „Amazing Grace“ hatte ursprünglich sechs Strophen, und die letzte Strophe wurde etwa ein Jahrhundert später hinzugefügt. Die meisten Gesangbücher enthalten vier oder fünf dieser Strophen.

Als Geistlicher in der Kirche wurde John durch den weiterhin betriebenen Sklavenhandel zunehmend beunruhigt. Im Jahr 1788, 34 Jahre nachdem er den Sklavenhandel verlassen hatte, schrieb er ein Buch mit dem Titel Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade und sandte es an alle Parlamentsmitglieder. Dieses Buch machte der Öffentlichkeit die Übel des Sklavenhandels bewusst. Er führt folgendes Zitat an: „Es versteht sich von selbst, dass das Gefangennehmen, Verkaufen und Transportieren schwarzer Sklaven auf die Plantagen in Westindien und Amerika eine grausame und bösartige Lebensweise war.“ Mit Gottes Hilfe und Vorsehung erlebte John im Jahr 1807, mehrere Monate vor seinem Tod, den Tag, an dem die Sklaverei offiziell aus England verbannt wurde.

Als John in seinen Sechzigern war, starb seine geliebte Frau Mary. Dies war eine schwere Prüfung für John, und er verbrachte die verbleibenden 17 Jahre seines Lebens ohne sie.

Nachdem John einen Schlaganfall erlitten hatte und kurz vor seinem Tod, ermutigte ihn ein Sprecher der Kirche, wegen seiner nachlassenden Gesundheit, Sehkraft und Erinnerungskraft darüber nachzudenken, das Predigen aufzugeben. John antwortete: „Was, soll der alte afrikanische Gotteslästerer aufhören, solange er noch sprechen kann? Ich werde weiter predigen. Obwohl mein Gedächtnis nachlässt, erinnere ich mich an zwei Dinge ganz deutlich: Ich bin ein großer Sünder, und Christus ist ein großer Erlöser.“

John Newtons letzte Worte auf seinem Sterbebett lauteten: „Ich bin noch im Land der Sterbenden; bald werde ich im Land der Lebenden sein.“

Die Melodie von „Amazing Grace“ ist eine frühe amerikanische Volksweise. Sie war zuerst als Plantagenmelodie mit dem Titel „Liebende Lämmer“ bekannt. Diese Melodie wurde erstmals 1831 in dem Buch The Virginia Harmony veröffentlicht. Die meisten danach veröffentlichten Gesangbücher enthielten dieses Lied. Im Jahr 1910 fügte Edwin O. Excell die letzte Strophe hinzu, die schließlich die letzten drei ursprünglichen Strophen des Liedes ersetzte. Seine Fassung des Liedes ist heute in unseren Gesangbüchern am weitesten verbreitet. Mehrere andere Lieder Newtons aus den Olney Hymns werden noch heute gesungen, darunter „Wie lieblich klingt der Name Jesu“ und „Herrliches wird von dir gesagt“.

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Ni jambo la kushangaza mno kwamba Mungu anaweza kumchukua mwenye dhambi mnyonge, asiye na hofu ya Bwana, na kumgeuza kuwa mtakatifu aliyeoshwa kwa damu na mhubiri wa injili! Katika simulizi hili, tunaona nguvu za Mungu zinazobadili maisha zikifanya kazi katika maisha ya mwandishi wetu wa tenzi.

Katika makaburi madogo yaliyo kwenye uwanja wa kanisa huko Olney, Uingereza, kuna jiwe la kaburi la graniti lenye maandishi haya, yaliyoandikwa na Newton mwenyewe kabla ya kifo chake:

John Newton, ambaye zamani alikuwa asiyeamini na mwenye maisha ya uasherati, mtumishi wa watumwa barani Afrika, kwa rehema nyingi za Bwana na Mwokozi wetu Yesu Kristo, alihifadhiwa, akarejeshwa, akasamehewa, na kuteuliwa kuhubiri imani ambayo kwa muda mrefu alikuwa amejitahidi kuiangamiza!

Maandishi haya ya kaburini yanaeleza vizuri maisha yasiyo ya kawaida na yaliyojaa matukio ya mtu huyu, mmoja wa wahubiri wakuu wa kiinjili wa karne ya kumi na nane. Ushuhuda wake ulikuwa, “Kwa neema ya Mungu, mimi ni hivi nilivyo!”

“Neema ya Ajabu” ni wimbo uliochapishwa mwaka 1779, wenye maneno yaliyoandikwa mwaka 1772 na mshairi Mwingereza na kasisi wa Kianglikana John Newton (1725–1807). Huenda “Neema ya Ajabu” ndio wimbo unaopendwa zaidi katika karne mbili zilizopita. Inakadiriwa kwamba wimbo huu huimbwa au kuchezwa mara milioni 10 kila mwaka. Umeonekana kwenye albamu zaidi ya 11,000 na kutafsiriwa katika lugha karibu 60. Ulitajwa katika riwaya ya Harriet Beecher Stowe inayopinga utumwa, Uncle Tom’s Cabin. Umaarufu wake uliongezeka sana wakati wa majanga mawili makubwa zaidi ya Marekani: Vita vya Wenyewe kwa Wenyewe na Vita vya Vietnam.

Kwa namna ya kushangaza, wimbo huu unaogusa moyo, unaohusishwa kwa karibu na jamii ya Waamerika wenye asili ya Afrika, uliandikwa na mtu aliyekuwa mfanyabiashara wa watumwa, John Newton.

John alizaliwa tarehe 24 Julai 1725, huko Wapping, Uingereza, kwa baba aliyekuwa baharia, John Newton, Sr., na mama aliyekuwa Mkristo mwenye bidii, Elizabeth Newton. Baba yake alimpenda lakini muda mwingi alikuwa baharini. Kwa upande mwingine, mama yake alikuwa mpole na mwenye kumlea kwa upendo, akimfundisha Neno la Mungu. Alimfundisha kukariri Biblia kwa sura nzima moja baada ya nyingine na kumpeleka kanisani. Kwa bahati mbaya, alipokaribia kutimiza miaka saba, mama yake alikufa kwa kifua kikuu. Baba yake alioa tena muda mfupi baadaye na kumpeleka shule ya bweni. Akiwa shuleni humo, alipata marafiki wabaya. Tabia yake iliharibika kiasi kwamba alifukuzwa katika shule moja na kuhamishiwa nyingine. Alipofikisha umri wa miaka 11, shule za bweni hazikumtaka, hivyo baba yake akaenda naye baharini. Alitumia miaka sita iliyofuata katika Bahari ya Atlantiki pamoja na baba yake.

John alipokuwa na miaka 17, baba yake alipanga kumpeleka Jamaica kwa kazi yenye mshahara mzuri ya kusimamia shamba kubwa. Akiwa njiani, alipokuwa akisubiri meli iondoke, John alipata mwaliko wa kwenda nyumbani kwa marafiki wa zamani, familia ya Catlett. Ni katika nyumba hiyo ambapo mama yake John alikuwa amefariki miaka kumi iliyotangulia. Alipokuwa akifahamiana nao tena, alimjua binti yao, Mary. Mama zake John na Mary walikuwa marafiki wa karibu sana. John alikuwa amealikwa kukaa siku nne, lakini alikaa wiki mbili na kuachwa na meli ya kwenda Jamaica.

Akiwa na umri wa miaka 18, John aliandikishwa kwa lazima katika Jeshi la Wanamaji la Kifalme, na maisha yake yakazidi kuwa mabaya. Alitaka kurudi kumwona Mary, hivyo akatoroka melini, lakini alikamatwa, akapigwa mijeledi hadharani, na kufungwa kwa minyororo ya chuma. Maisha yake melini yalikuwa ya kufuru kiasi kwamba hata mabaharia wengine wasiomcha Mungu walishtushwa na matusi na kufuru zake. Alipewa jina “Mkufuru Mkuu” na alikuwa mtu asiyetakiwa melini kiasi kwamba alitumwa kufanya kazi katika meli ya watumwa.

Mmoja wa wamiliki wa meli ya watumwa ambamo sasa alikuwa akifanya kazi alimwahidi John kazi mara tu watakapofika pwani ya Afrika. Hata hivyo, alipofika nchi kavu, alifungwa na kulazimishwa kufanya kazi akiwa na chakula, mavazi, na makazi haba. Wakati huo alimtumia baba yake barua kadhaa, akiomba msaada kwa kusihi.

Meli iliyoitwa The Greyhound ilikuwa ikisafiri karibu na pwani ambayo sasa John alikuwa akiita nyumbani. Nahodha alikuwa ameagizwa na baba yake John amtafute mwanawe. Ingawa meli ilikuwa karibu mbali mno na ufuo kufanya biashara, waliamua kujaribu kufanya biashara. Rafiki mmoja wa John alipiga makasia kutoka ufuoni kwenda kufanya biashara. Alipogeuka kuondoka, nahodha alimuuliza ikiwa alimjua mtu aliyeitwa John Newton. Kwa mshangao wa nahodha, alimjua, na John akaletwa melini ili arudi nyumbani.

Akiwa melini, Newton alichukua nakala ya kitabu maarufu cha Kikristo cha Thomas á Kempis, The Imitation of Christ. Hakuwahi kukutana na kitu kama hicho, na akaanza kujiuliza kama madai ya Ukristo yanaweza kuwa ya kweli. Usiku huo, tarehe 10 Machi 1748, dhoruba kali ilikaribia kuizamisha meli. Watu, wanyama, na mahitaji ya safari yalisombwa na kutupwa baharini. Dhoruba ilimwamsha Newton, huku mbao zilizooza za meli zikivunjwa na mawimbi na maji yakizunguka na kuingia katika chumba chake. John aliomba kwa mara ya kwanza baada ya miaka mingi.

The Greyhound ilirushwa huku na huku katika dhoruba ya Atlantiki ya Kaskazini kwa zaidi ya siku 11. Wakiwa na tumaini dogo la kuokoka, mabaharia waliendesha pampu kwa mazoea tu, wakijaribu kuifanya meli iendelee kuelea. Katika siku ya kumi na moja ya dhoruba, John alikuwa amechoka sana asiweze kusukuma pampu, hivyo akafungwa kwenye usukani, ambako alijitahidi kadiri alivyoweza kuifanya meli ibaki kwenye njia yake. Kuanzia saa saba mchana hadi usiku wa manane, alikuwa kwenye usukani. Aliogopa kwamba angekufa, na kama imani ya Kikristo ilikuwa ya kweli, basi bila shaka asingesamehewa. Alitafakari yote aliyokuwa amefanya katika miaka michache iliyopita. Maisha yake yalionekana kuharibika na kuvunjika kama meli iliyopigwa vibaya ambayo alikuwa akijaribu kuiongoza katika dhoruba. Katika saa hizo ndefu na zenye kuchosha sana, Newton alimlilia Mungu kwa namna ambayo hakuwahi kufanya hapo awali, na huo ukawa wakati wa mabadiliko makubwa katika maisha yake.

Hiyo ilikuwa siku ambayo John Newton aliikumbuka daima baadaye. “Siku hiyo, Bwana alituma msaada kutoka juu na kuniokoa katika maji yenye kina kirefu.” Zaidi ya miaka 50 baadaye, John aliandika katika shajara yake tarehe 21 Machi 1805: “Siwezi kuandika vizuri; lakini ninajitahidi kuadhimisha kurudi kwa siku hii kwa kujinyenyekeza, maombi, na sifa.”

Ni neema ya ajabu ya Mungu pekee ambayo ingeweza kumchukua baharia mkorofi, mwenye kufuru, mfanyabiashara wa watumwa, na kumgeuza kuwa mtoto wa Mungu. John hakuacha kamwe kustaajabia kazi ya Mungu katika maisha yake. Alianza kupendezwa na maombi, kusoma na kutafakari Maandiko, na kusema maneno yanayompendeza Mungu pekee.

Aliporudi nyumbani, Mary na wazazi wake walitambua mabadiliko ambayo Bwana alikuwa ameleta ndani ya John. Wawili hao walioana tarehe 1 Februari 1750.

Kwa miaka minne iliyofuata, Newton alikuwa nahodha wa meli yake mwenyewe ya watumwa. Kazi hii ilimtenganisha na Mary kwa miezi kadhaa kila mara. Walipokuwa mbali, wawili hao waliandikiana barua daima. Katika barua zake, John aliandika mara kwa mara jinsi upendo na ndoa yao zilivyoongeza shukrani zake kwa Bwana. “... Ninapojipa nafasi ya kukuwaza kwa namna ya pekee, kwa kawaida mawazo hayo hunipeleka mbali zaidi na kunifanya nipige magoti kumhimidi Bwana kwa kunipa hazina kama hii na kuombea amani na ustawi wako”

John alijitahidi kuifanya meli yake ya watumwa iwe ya “Kikristo” kwa kuendesha ibada za Jumapili kwa wafanyakazi wake 30 waliokuwa wameshupazwa na dhambi. Alifanya safari nyingine tatu kuleta watumwa kutoka Afrika kwenda Amerika ya Kaskazini. Alipokuwa akipanga safari yake ya nne, aliugua malaria. Mungu alitumia ugonjwa huu kukomesha ushiriki wake katika biashara ya watumwa.

John alipoanza ukurasa mpya wa maisha yake, alihisi kuwa ameitwa kuwa mhudumu wa kanisa. Kwa zaidi ya miaka 50, alihubiri injili na alikuwa mmoja wa watu wenye ushawishi mkubwa zaidi wa wakati wake.

Mara nyingi John Newton alitunga wimbo uendane na ibada zake za Jumapili jioni. Mwaka 1779, nyimbo 280 kati ya hizo zilikusanywa na kuunganishwa na nyimbo 68 za rafiki wa Newton na mshiriki wa parokia yake, William Cowper, na kuchapishwa kama Olney Hymns. Wimbo maarufu zaidi kati ya Olney Hymns zote, “Kutazama Nyuma na Matarajio ya Imani”, ulitokana na mshangao wa Daudi katika 1 Mambo ya Nyakati 17:16-17. Leo tunaujua kama “Neema ya Ajabu”. Awali “Neema ya Ajabu” ulikuwa na beti sita, na ubeti wa mwisho uliongezwa karibu karne moja baadaye. Vitabu vingi vya tenzi vina beti nne au tano kati ya hizo.

Akiwa mhudumu katika kanisa, John aliendelea kusumbuliwa zaidi na zaidi na biashara ya watumwa iliyokuwa bado ikiendelea. Mwaka 1788, miaka 34 baada ya kuacha biashara ya watumwa, aliandika kitabu kilichoitwa Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade na kukituma kwa wabunge wote. Kitabu hiki kiliwafanya watu wafahamu maovu ya biashara ya watumwa. Ananukuu hivi, “Bila shaka, kuwakamata, kuwauza na kuwasafirisha watumwa weusi kwenda kwenye mashamba makubwa katika visiwa vya West Indies na Amerika ilikuwa njia ya maisha ya ukatili na uovu.” Kwa msaada na uongozi wa Mungu, John aliiona siku, miezi kadhaa kabla ya kifo chake mwaka 1807, ambapo utumwa ulipigwa marufuku rasmi nchini Uingereza.

John alipokuwa katika miaka yake ya sitini, mke wake mpendwa Mary alifariki. Hili lilikuwa jaribu kubwa kwa John, naye alitumia miaka 17 iliyobaki ya maisha yake bila yeye.

Baada ya John kupata kiharusi na muda mfupi kabla ya kifo chake, msemaji wa kanisa alimhimiza Newton afikirie kustaafu kuhubiri kwa sababu afya, uwezo wa kuona, na kumbukumbu zake zilikuwa zikidhoofika. John alijibu, “Eti nini, yule mkufuru wa zamani wa Afrika aache wakati bado anaweza kusema? Nitaendelea kuhubiri. Ingawa kumbukumbu zangu zinafifia, ninakumbuka mambo mawili kwa uwazi kabisa: Mimi ni mwenye dhambi mkubwa, na Kristo ni Mwokozi mkuu.”

Maneno ya mwisho ya John Newton alipokuwa amelala kitandani akikaribia kufa yalikuwa haya: “Bado niko katika nchi ya wanaokufa; hivi karibuni nitakuwa katika nchi ya walio hai.”

Melodia ya “Neema ya Ajabu” ni melodia ya zamani ya kimapokeo ya Marekani. Kwanza ilijulikana kama melodia ya mashambani iliyoitwa “Wanakondoo Wenye Upendo”. Melodia hii ilichapishwa kwa mara ya kwanza mwaka 1831 katika kitabu The Virginia Harmony. Vitabu vingi vya tenzi vilivyochapishwa baada ya wakati huo vilijumuisha wimbo huu. Mwaka 1910, Edwin O. Excell aliongeza ubeti wa mwisho, ambao hatimaye ulichukua nafasi ya beti tatu za mwisho za awali za wimbo huo. Toleo lake la wimbo ndilo linalopatikana zaidi katika vitabu vyetu vya tenzi leo. Nyimbo nyingine kadhaa za Newton katika Olney hymns zinaendelea kuimbwa leo, zikiwemo “Jinsi Jina la Yesu Linavyosikika kwa Utamu” na “Mambo ya Utukufu Yanasemwa Kukuhusu”.

“Dr. Waldron, Elsie needs help!” Elsie’s husband was adamant, almost angry, as he stared at me. On the other hand, Elsie stared at the floor, almost as though she wasn’t present. I had never met either of the couple before and was struggling just a little to figure out what was needed from me to help her.

“What is going on?” I asked as I flipped through her chart. This was still in the days of paper charts, and I headed to the lab section of her chart. There wasn’t anything too crazy that I could see there—her liver enzymes were a little elevated, but otherwise, everything seemed OK.

“It’s her drinking!” Her husband told me. “She is drinking more and more every night. She won’t go out except to get whiskey. She drinks till she passes out every night and has to have something every morning to get her started.”

“Is that true?” I asked Elsie, feeling like a judge overseeing a jury trial.

“Yes,” she said. Her face was emotionless, and I couldn’t tell if she wanted to be there or not.

“Do you want help?” I asked her. This was a loaded question. Many people who struggle with alcoholism aren’t ready to break free from its vice-like hold on them. Maybe Elsie was different.

“I guess so,” she said, indifferently. Once again, I couldn’t tell whether she wanted to be there or not.

“At the rate at which you are drinking, you will kill yourself within a year – maybe two at best – if you don’t give up alcohol entirely,” I told her. “If you want to, I will try to find you an inpatient program to detox you and get you off of alcohol.”

“She’s ready,” he husband said firmly.

When dealing with someone who drinks heavily, it is crucial that they don’t simply stop drinking without medical support. Abrupt cessation of alcohol use causes the body to go into withdrawal which can produce a state called Delirium Tremens and even seizures.

I stepped out of the exam room and to make phone calls. It is never easy to find a place for someone to attempt to rehabilitate from any kind of substances, and it was over an hour and a half before I found a facility that was willing to take Elsie and try to help her get off of the whiskey.

I sighed as I reentered her exam room. I had been afraid that I wouldn’t find anywhere for her to go.

I told them about the plan, and her husband nodded vigorously, while Elise continued to stare silently at the floor. “Can we pray together before you go?” I asked them, and when they nodded assent, I prayed with them, asking for freedom and Jesus’ presence in both of their lives.

They left my office with marching orders and directions on where to go. I had a happy glow about me for the rest of the morning, knowing that I had gone the extra mile and had really made a difference in this middle-aged couple’s life.

Around 2 pm, I got a call from the rehab facility. They hadn’t seen even a shadow of Elsie or her husband, which was surprising, since it was a bright sunny day and the facility wasn’t that far away. With a sinking feeling, I dialed the couple’s phone number.

“She won’t go!” Her husband told me. “She tells me that she told me this ahead of time. She’ll try to cut back, but she isn’t willing to go into a rehab facility or any such thing. I guess just tell them that we’ll let them know if she changes her mind.”

My nurse called the rehab facility and told them the bad news, and I sat down in my chair, stunned. What else could I have done? Was there a solution for Elsie—something different that I could have said that would have made a difference in her life?

About a year later, I received the sad news that Elsie had died at home. I was certain that things would have been different if she had gone to rehab and if she had given control to Jesus. None of that had happened, and I felt cynicism pushing into my heart.

Cynicism

We live in an age of cynicism. In ancient Greece, the cynics were an odd assortment of men who specialized in being grouchy and saying mean (they would have said truthful) things to people. They often dressed in rags and behaved in such a way that most of the polite Athenians did not want to be close to them.

Today, cynicism means a tendency to believe the worst about people and circumstances. Cynical people believe that all people are motivated purely by selfishness and that bad events will tend to prevail.

Many young doctors are idealistic and very hopeful. They believe that if they exert the utmost effort, they can make a real, positive impact on their patient’s lives. Unfortunately, as time goes by and they try their hardest and their patients don’t change, they can give up. These doctors still try, but they no longer really hope that their efforts will make much of a difference.

It seems as though people who get involved with politics often have the best of intentions. They see this as a path to changing society for the better. Unfortunately, as time goes by and the faces in charge change, the policies don’t really change, they tend to become cynical.

Sometimes this cynicism is directed against all politicians. Sometimes it is only anger directed against members of the party that opposes their party’s positions. Hope is replaced by cynicism.

Cynicism in the Bible

If there is a book in the Bible that seems to have been written by a cynical man, it is the book of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who we understand to be Solomon, lists all of the things that he endeavored in an attempt to find joy.

In chapter 2:17-23 Solomon describes work as futile. He finishes by saying, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

He saw the world as being dominated by tyrants and there was little that the people could do about it. Solomon went so far as to say that political power was meaningless “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiastes 6:6, he seems to disparage long life. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Of course, he finishes his short book with the instruction to remember our Creator in the days of our youth. There is a blessing for those who choose to focus on God when they have a little bit of energy left and not, when they are old and jaded, like Solomon.

Later on, it almost seemed as though God had given up on His people. He still sent prophets to them, but He knew without a doubt that the people would refuse to respond. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Even in the New Testament, Paul told Timothy that the time was coming when people would no longer listen to sound doctrine. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

By picking and choosing these passages, we can come away with a very gloomy view of the future and, more specifically, of human’s willingness to change. It seems there is little point of investing ourselves in the people around us. They are full of woe and are as likely to change as a chipmunk is to master differential calculus.

The Opposite of Cynicism

The opposite of cynicism is hope. It is the belief that the future could be better.

It is interesting that the Apostle Paul spoke of tribulations in the Epistle to the Romans, “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

We may not have reached the place where we glory in the trials we experience, but certainly, they should bring us these other things that he mentions. For, we grow in patience and experience, even as we deal with trials, but more than that, we come to realize that we have hope for tomorrow because we serve a great God.

The contrast in the story of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15 teaches us much about hope. The father and the older brother were strikingly different in their attitudes.

The father had never given up hope – he knew that his son had failed him and gone far from what he knew was right and yet, the father still desired to see the prodigal come to himself and return home.

On the other hand, the older brother not only had no hope for his younger brother, but he was also angry with him. The prodigal had wasted his money, he had lived in sin, and now, he had returned home just because he was out of money.

Certainly, there was no reason to trust the younger son. Yet, that is exactly what our Heavenly Father does for us.

Look for Hope in the Right Places

Part of the problem is that we look for hope in the wrong places. A number of years ago, a presidential candidate ran for office under the slogan “Hope and Change,” and yet, even though he was elected, I imagine most folks did not feel that their lives were significantly changed for the better.

Pursuing the things this world values—political power and wealth is guaranteed to bring emptiness. This is Satan’s pattern—he always over-promises and under-delivers.

This was what he did when he tempted Jesus, “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). All of the things Satan offered, nothing compared with the glory that Jesus eventually received from the road that led to the cross.

In the same way, Satan would like to distract Christians from seeking the things that are valuable, and that will bring hope. Satan tells Christians that politics will not only change the world for the better, it is an easier way to change the world.

The Bible is clear that we build hope as we nurture our relationship with God and then work to help our brothers and sisters build that same relationship in their own lives. The reason that we can hope is not because people are so wonderful—we don’t have to live very long to realize that they aren’t. The reason we hope is because we serve an awesome, faithful God who walks with us through the worst of our trials.

Remember that We Have Undeserved Hope

Jesus’ messages about forgiveness make it clear that one of the major reasons that we have for forgiving others in our lives is that we have received great and undeserved forgiveness. The same is true for hope.

Each one of us was hopeless and without reason to expect to receive hope and we were still given a ray of light in the midst of our darkness. Maybe part of the reason that we have so much trouble hoping for good things for the people around us is that we do not remember how hopeless we were before we found grace.

If Jesus was able to bring hope to our hopeless existence, then certainly He can do wonderful things in the hearts and lives of others around us. The only people we should give up on are the ones that our Savior has given up on as well.

Small Efforts Do Make a Difference

I remember having a conversation with a young person who was planning to go into medicine and had a plan to go to a foreign country and serve the people there. As we were talking, an older man entered the conversation and shared that he saw little hope for change in developing countries.

The people in those countries just weren’t interested in getting better and didn’t do the minimum necessary to stave off things like worms and parasites. Doctors and nurses couldn’t make a difference in such an environment.

I could sense the heart of the youth sinking as this older man shared. He had experience, and he had given up hope. The sad thing was that he was also stealing the hope of someone who still had a desire to serve.

When I was in training, I had a surgeon tell me that family doctors didn’t really do anything. They simply kept their patients alive till their next office visit, whereas surgeons really “fixed” people—taking out (or off) the offending body part.

At the end of the day, small efforts do make a difference. I don’t do brain surgery, but I still can make a difference in someone else’s life— maybe just by spending a little time and listening and praying. This is true for all of us.

More than that, we come to realize that making this effort changes our own lives for the better. Jesus told the sheep that as they ministered to “the least of these my brethren,” they were ministering to Him.

Even if no one’s life is improved, our Savior knows our desires and feels our efforts, and will reward them someday.

A Few Things to Remember

When we face failures, we tend to move in one of two directions. Those of us who are optimists tend to believe that this episode was an isolated event and that the future is still bright. On the other hand, pessimists believe that failures are permanent, personal, and pervasive.

Pessimists believe that their failures are the result of intrinsic character flaws that they have and that these things affect all of their lives and are unlikely to change. Unlike the righteous man who falls to rise again, these people fall and lie where they fall, defeated at the outset.

When we are dealing with other people, we need to give them the same grace that we should give ourselves. They, too, are growing, and if they have a failure today, they will do better tomorrow. Maybe they will fail again, but they will at least “fail better.”

Conclusion

Cynicism is rife in our world. Many have given up hope for a better future, and it is understandable for those who have invested their hope in this world’s institutions. There is no real hope in government or in armies or in bureaucracy.

The song says, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” For, Jesus is the one who brings light into our darkness and allows us to continue, even when others fail us.

God is the one who redeems us. He is the one who sent the prophets, even though their messages were ignored, and the prophets were persecuted. He is the one who continues to hope for us, even when we have failed Him so many times in the past.

He is the reason we carry on. He is the reason that we have hope, not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.

“沃尔德伦医生，埃尔西需要帮助！”埃尔西的丈夫盯着我，态度坚决，几乎带着怒气。埃尔西却盯着地板，仿佛人不在这里。我以前从未见过这对夫妇，一时有些摸不清，要帮助她究竟需要我做些什么。

“出了什么事？”我一边翻阅她的病历，一边问道。那时还在使用纸质病历，我翻到了化验记录的部分。我没有发现什么特别异常的情况——她的肝酶略有升高，但除此之外，一切看起来都还好。

“是她喝酒的问题！”她丈夫告诉我。“她每晚喝得越来越多。除了买威士忌，她根本不出门。她每天晚上都喝到不省人事，每天早晨还得喝点酒才能开始一天的生活。”

“是这样吗？”我问埃尔西，感觉自己像个主持陪审团审判的法官。

“是的，”她说。她脸上毫无表情，我看不出她是否愿意来这里。

“你想得到帮助吗？”我问她。这是个分量很重的问题。许多深陷酒瘾的人还没有准备好挣脱酒精对他们如虎钳般的控制。也许埃尔西会不一样。

“大概吧，”她冷淡地说。我仍然看不出她是否愿意来这里。

“照你现在这样喝下去，如果不彻底戒酒，一年之内你就会把自己的命喝掉——最多也许两年，”我告诉她。“如果你愿意，我会尽力为你找一个住院治疗项目，帮助你度过戒断期，戒掉酒精。”

“她准备好了，”她丈夫坚定地说。

面对一个大量饮酒的人，至关重要的是，不能让他们在没有医疗支持的情况下就直接停酒。突然停止饮酒会使身体出现戒断反应，可能引发一种叫作震颤谵妄的状态，甚至导致癫痫发作。

我走出诊室去打电话。为需要戒除任何成瘾物质的人找到康复治疗的地方，从来都不容易。过了一个半小时多，我才找到一家愿意接收埃尔西、尝试帮助她戒掉威士忌的机构。

重新走进诊室时，我叹了口气。我一直担心找不到任何可以让她去的地方。

我把计划告诉他们，她丈夫使劲点头，埃莉斯却依然默默地盯着地板。“你们走之前，我们能一起祷告吗？”我问他们。他们点头同意后，我便与他们一起祷告，求主使他们得自由，也求耶稣与他们两人的生命同在。

他们带着明确的行动指示和前往那里的路线离开了我的诊所。那天上午余下的时间，我心里一直洋溢着喜悦，因为我知道自己多付出了努力，确实为这对中年夫妇的生活带来了改变。

下午两点左右，康复机构给我打来电话。他们连埃尔西或她丈夫的影子都没见到。这很令人意外，因为那天天气晴朗，阳光明媚，而且那家机构离得并不远。我心里一沉，拨通了这对夫妇的电话。

“她不肯去！”她丈夫告诉我。“她说她早就跟我说过了。她会试着少喝一点，但她不愿意进康复机构，也不愿意接受诸如此类的安排。我想，你就告诉他们，要是她改变主意，我们会通知他们。”

我的护士打电话把这个坏消息告诉了康复机构，我则呆呆地坐进椅子里。我还能做些什么呢？有没有能帮助埃尔西的办法——我是否可以换一种说法，从而改变她的生活？

大约一年后，我得知了埃尔西在家中去世的噩耗。我确信，如果她去了康复机构，如果她把掌管权交给耶稣，事情就会不一样。然而，这两件事都没有发生，我感到愤世嫉俗的情绪正侵入我的内心。

愤世嫉俗

我们生活在一个愤世嫉俗的时代。在古希腊，犬儒派是一群古怪的人，他们专门向人发牢骚，说些刻薄的话（他们自己会说那是真话）。他们常常衣衫褴褛，举止也让大多数彬彬有礼的雅典人不愿靠近他们。

如今，愤世嫉俗指的是一种倾向，即总把人和处境往最坏的方面想。愤世嫉俗的人认为，所有人的动机都纯粹出于自私，而坏事往往会占上风。

许多年轻医生怀抱理想，满怀希望。他们相信，只要竭尽全力，就能给病人的生活带来真正积极的影响。可惜，随着时间过去，他们已经尽了最大努力，病人却没有改变，他们便可能放弃。这些医生仍然在努力，却不再真正期望自己的努力能带来多大的改变。

参与政治的人似乎往往怀着最好的初衷。他们把政治看作一条让社会变得更好的道路。可惜，随着时间过去，掌权的人换了，政策却没有真正改变，他们往往就变得愤世嫉俗。

有时，这种愤世嫉俗针对的是所有政治人物。有时，它只是针对那些与自己所属政党的立场相对立的政党成员的怒气。愤世嫉俗取代了希望。

圣经中的愤世嫉俗

如果圣经中有一卷书看起来像是由一个愤世嫉俗的人写成的，那就是《传道书》。我们认为其中的传道者就是所罗门，他列举了自己为寻求喜乐而尝试的一切事情。

在第2:17-23节中，所罗门将工作描述为徒劳。他最后说：“人在日光之下劳碌，心中烦忧，他这一切的劳碌究竟给他带来什么呢？因为他一生的日子都是忧愁，他的劳苦都是悲伤；甚至夜间，他的心也不得安歇。这也是虚空。”（传道书2:22,23）

他看见世界被暴君统治，而百姓几乎无能为力。所罗门甚至说，政治权力毫无意义：“贫穷而有智慧的少年，胜过年老而愚昧、不再肯接受劝诫的君王。因为他从监牢出来作王；而那生在自己国中的，也会变得贫穷。”（传道书4:13）

在传道书6:6中，他似乎贬低长寿的价值。“即使他活了一千年的两倍，却没有见过福乐，众人岂不都归到同一个地方吗？”

当然，他在这卷短书的结尾，教导我们要在年轻的日子记念创造我们的主。那些选择在还剩一些精力时就专注于上帝，而不是像所罗门那样，等到年老、厌倦一切时才这样做的人，是有福的。

后来，上帝几乎像是已经放弃了祂的子民。祂仍然向他们差遣先知，但祂毫无疑问地知道，这些人会拒绝回应。“所以，你要把这一切话告诉他们，他们却不听从你；你也要呼唤他们，他们却不回答你。”（耶利米书7:27）

即使在新约中，保罗也告诉提摩太，时候将到，人们不再听从纯正的教导。“因为时候将到，他们不肯容忍纯正的教导，反倒因耳朵发痒，照着自己的欲望，为自己聚集许多教师；”（提摩太后书4:3）

如果挑选这些经文来读，我们可能对未来产生非常阴暗的看法，尤其是对人愿不愿意改变的看法。这样看来，把自己投入到身边的人身上似乎没什么意义。他们满是愁苦，要他们改变，就像要一只花栗鼠精通微分学一样不可能。

愤世嫉俗的反面

愤世嫉俗的反面是盼望，是相信未来可以更好。

有趣的是，使徒保罗在《罗马书》中谈到了患难：“不但如此，我们也以患难为荣；因为知道患难产生忍耐，忍耐产生老练，老练产生盼望；盼望不会使人蒙羞，因为上帝的爱藉着赐给我们的圣灵，倾注在我们心里。”（罗马书5:3-5）

我们也许还没有达到以自己经历的试炼为荣的地步，但试炼当然应当给我们带来他所提到的其他这些品质。因为即使在应对试炼时，我们也在忍耐和老练上成长。更重要的是，我们逐渐认识到，自己对明天有盼望，因为我们所事奉的是一位伟大的上帝。

路加福音15章浪子故事中的对比，教导了我们许多有关盼望的事。父亲和哥哥的态度截然不同。

父亲从未放弃盼望——他知道儿子辜负了他，远远偏离了自己明知是正确的道路，然而，父亲依然渴望看见浪子醒悟过来，回到家中。

另一方面，哥哥不仅对弟弟没有盼望，而且还对他满怀怒气。浪子挥霍了钱财，活在罪中，如今只是因为钱花光了才回家。

的确，没有理由信任这个小儿子。然而，我们的天父对我们所做的，恰恰就是如此。

在正确的地方寻找盼望

问题部分在于，我们在错误的地方寻找盼望。若干年前，一位总统候选人以“希望与变革”为口号竞选。然而，尽管他当选了，我想大多数人并没有觉得自己的生活明显变好了。

追求这个世界所看重的东西——政治权力和财富——必定带来空虚。这就是撒但的惯常做法：他总是承诺过多，兑现过少。

他试探耶稣时就是这样做的：“你若俯伏敬拜我，我就把这一切都赐给你。”（马太福音4:8）撒但所提供的一切，没有一样能与耶稣最终沿着通往十字架的道路所获得的荣耀相比。

同样，撒但想使基督徒分心，不去追求那些有价值、能带来盼望的事物。撒但告诉基督徒，政治不但能让世界变得更好，而且是改变世界的一条更轻松的道路。

圣经清楚表明，当我们培育自己与上帝的关系，并努力帮助弟兄姐妹在他们的生命中建立同样的关系时，盼望就会增长。我们能够盼望，并不是因为人有多么美好——我们不必活很久就会发现，人并非如此。我们怀有盼望，是因为我们所事奉的是一位令人敬畏、信实的上帝，祂在我们最艰难的试炼中与我们同行。

记得我们拥有本不配得的盼望

耶稣关于饶恕的教导清楚表明，我们饶恕生活中他人的一个主要原因，是我们已经领受了极大、且本不配得的饶恕。盼望也是如此。

我们每一个人原本都毫无盼望，也没有理由期待得到盼望，然而，我们仍然在黑暗中蒙赐一线光明。也许，我们之所以很难盼望身边的人得着好事，部分原因就在于，我们不记得自己在找到恩典之前，是多么没有盼望。

如果耶稣能为我们毫无盼望的生命带来盼望，祂当然也能在我们身边其他人的心中和生命中成就美好的事。我们唯一应当放弃的人，就是我们的救主也已经放弃的人。

微小的努力确实能带来改变

我记得曾和一位年轻人交谈，他打算从医，也计划去国外服事那里的人。我们谈话时，一位年长的男士加入进来，说他认为发展中国家几乎没有改变的希望。

那些国家的人根本不想变得更好，连预防蠕虫和寄生虫之类问题所需的最低限度措施也不愿做。在这样的环境中，医生和护士不可能带来改变。

听着这位年长者的话，我能感觉到那年轻人的心越来越沉重。这位年长者有经验，却已经放弃了盼望。可悲的是，他也在夺走一个仍然渴望服事之人的盼望。

我接受培训时，一位外科医生曾告诉我，家庭医生其实没做什么。他们只不过是让病人活到下次来诊，而外科医生才真正把人“修好”——把出问题的身体部位切除或截掉。

归根结底，微小的努力确实能带来改变。我不做脑部手术，却仍然能够改变别人的生活——也许只是花一点时间倾听和祷告。我们每个人都是如此。

更进一步，我们逐渐认识到，付出这样的努力也会使我们自己的生命变得更好。耶稣告诉那些绵羊，他们服事“我这些弟兄中最微小的”，就是在服事祂。

即使没有任何人的生活得到改善，我们的救主仍知道我们的心愿，感受到我们的努力，并且有一天会给予赏赐。

几件需要记住的事

面对失败时，我们往往会走向两个方向之一。我们当中乐观的人往往相信，这次遭遇只是一个孤立事件，未来依然光明。另一方面，悲观的人则认为，失败是永久的、源于自身的，而且影响一切。

悲观的人认为，自己的失败源于内在的性格缺陷，这些缺陷影响着他们生活的方方面面，而且不太可能改变。他们不像那跌倒后又起来的义人，而是跌倒之后就躺在原地，一开始便认输了。

与他人相处时，我们需要给予他们同样的恩典，就像我们应当给予自己的一样。他们也在成长，今天若失败了，明天就会做得更好。也许他们还会失败，但至少会“失败得更好”。

结语

愤世嫉俗在我们的世界里盛行。许多人已经放弃了对更美好未来的盼望；对于那些把希望寄托在这个世界的制度和机构上的人来说，这是可以理解的。政府、军队和官僚体制中，都没有真正的盼望。

有首歌唱道：“啊，若在耶稣里没有盼望，这世界该是何等黑暗！”因为，正是耶稣为我们的黑暗带来光明，使我们即使在别人辜负我们时，也能继续前行。

上帝是救赎我们的那一位。差遣先知的是祂，尽管先知的信息被置之不理，先知也遭受迫害。即使我们过去多次辜负祂，仍然对我们怀有盼望的，也是祂。

祂是我们继续前行的原因。祂是我们怀有盼望的原因，不仅为自己，也为我们的弟兄。
