পরিস্থিতির কারণে অতিরিক্ত চাপে পড়া হয়তো সবচেয়ে কঠিন। আমাদের সময়সূচিতে কিছুটা অবসর রাখার প্রয়োজন হলে আমরা কোনো Norwex অনুষ্ঠানে না যাওয়ার সিদ্ধান্ত নিতে পারি। কিন্তু বিয়ের প্রস্তুতির মাঝখানে কোনো সন্তানের পা ভেঙে গেলে, পরিস্থিতি যতটা সম্ভব ভালোভাবে সামাল দেওয়া ছাড়া আমাদের আর কোনো উপায় থাকে না।

পরিস্থিতির কারণে অতিরিক্ত চাপ ধীরে ধীরে আসতে পারে, যেমন পরের ঘটনাটিতে দেখা যায়; আবার হঠাৎও আসতে পারে, যেমন কোনো দুর্ঘটনায় পরিবারের একজন আহত হলে।

বেকির বয়স ত্রিশের কোঠায়, আর তাঁর সাতটি সন্তানের সবার বয়স সতেরোর নিচে। কয়েক বছর আগে তাঁদের একটি মুরগির ঘর আগুনে পুড়ে যায়। তখন তাঁরা কৃতজ্ঞ ছিলেন যে আগের দিনই মুরগিগুলো সরিয়ে নেওয়া হয়েছিল এবং প্রোপেনের ট্যাংকটি বিস্ফোরিত হওয়ার সময় আশেপাশে কেউ ছিল না।

বেকি বলেন, “আমার স্বামী পুরুষের মতো দৃঢ়ভাবে এই বিপর্যয়ের মুখোমুখি হয়েছিলেন। তাঁর শান্ত মনোভাব আমাকে স্বস্তি দিয়েছিল। আমি নিশ্চিত ছিলাম যে আমরা আর্থিক দিকটা সামলে নিতে পারব এবং জীবন আগের মতোই চলবে। কিন্তু আমি ভুল ছিলাম। একেবারেই ভুল।”

“সময়ের সঙ্গে ধ্বংসস্তূপ পরিষ্কার করা হলো, আর রিক আবার ঘরটি তৈরি করার খোঁজখবর নিলেন। খরচের প্রস্তাবগুলো প্রত্যাশার চেয়ে বেশি ছিল, তাই তিনি কিছু কাজ নিজেই করার সিদ্ধান্ত নিলেন। আয় বাড়ানোর জন্য তিনি একটি খণ্ডকালীন চাকরিও নিলেন। আমাদের ছেলেরা সাহায্য করার মতো বড় হয়েছিল, তবু রিকের নির্দেশনা ছাড়া তারা বেশি কিছু করতে পারত না।”

“প্রথমে এই পরিবর্তনের টান অনুভব করলাম আমার মানিব্যাগে, কিন্তু এই ভেবে নিজেকে সান্ত্বনা দিলাম যে এটা কেবল সাময়িক। তারপর রিকের চোখের উজ্জ্বলতার জায়গায় এলো নিষ্প্রভ দৃষ্টি। তিনি আমাদের থেকে দূরে সরে যেতে লাগলেন। বুঝতে পারছিলাম, কিছু একটা ঠিক নেই, কিন্তু ঠিক কী, তা ধরতে পারছিলাম না।”

“এরপর এক বিশ্বাসী ভাই বুলগেরিয়ায় কিছু সময় কাটাতে যাওয়ায়, তাঁর সম্পাদকের দায়িত্বের শেষ চার মাসের কাজ শেষ করার জন্য রিককে নির্বাচিত করা হলো। সেদিন রাতে তিনি বাড়ি ফিরে কাঁদলেন। ‘আমি কী অবস্থার মধ্য দিয়ে যাচ্ছি, তা কি কেউই বোঝে না? যেদিকেই ফিরি, কিছু না কিছু কাজ আছে। ছেলেরা মাছ ধরতে যেতে চায়, তোমার কাপড় শুকানোর নতুন দড়ি দরকার, আর মুরগির ঘরটা ছয় মাসের মধ্যে শেষ করতে হবে! মানসিকভাবে আর একটি দায়িত্বও সামলানোর ক্ষমতা আমার নেই।’”

বেকি বললেন, “ওটাই ছিল সহ্যের সীমা ছাড়িয়ে যাওয়ার শেষ চাপ। মাঝরাতে তাঁকে হাই তুলতে শুনে এবং বুঝতে পেরে যে তিনি ঘুমাচ্ছেন না, আমি আতঙ্কিত হয়ে পড়লাম।”

“আমার কাছে স্পষ্ট হয়ে গেল যে আমার সবকিছু নিখুঁতভাবে করতে চাওয়া স্বামী অতিরিক্ত চাপে পড়েছেন। রিক ক্রমেই আমার ওপর আরও বেশি নির্ভর করতে লাগলেন। আমি নিজের দায়দায়িত্ব কমিয়ে দিলাম এবং সময় খালি রাখার চেষ্টা করলাম, যাতে তাঁর ভার কিছুটা কমাতে সাহায্য করার জন্য আমি পাশে থাকতে পারি।”

“আমার মনে হচ্ছিল, আমি যেন একজন উদ্ধারকর্মী, একজন মানুষকে ডুবে যাওয়া থেকে বাঁচানোর চেষ্টা করছি, অথচ নিজেও একটু বেশি জল গিলে ফেলছি। সংসারের অনেক দায়িত্ব আমার কাঁধে এসে পড়ল। তারপর আমাকে ‘বুলগেরিয়ায়-যেতে-থাকা’ মহিলার বদলে খাদ্য কমিটিতে দায়িত্ব নিতে বলা হলো।”

দুঃখের বিষয়, পরিস্থিতির কারণে সৃষ্ট চাপ প্রায়ই কারও চোখে পড়ে না। আরও খারাপ হলো, যিনি এই চাপের শিকার, তাঁকে ভুল বোঝা হতে পারে বা তাঁর সম্পর্কে ভুল বিচার করা হতে পারে। বেকি বললেন, “আমার সবচেয়ে অন্ধকার দিনটি এসেছিল যখন খাদ্য কমিটির অনুরোধ প্রত্যাখ্যান করায় আমাকে নিজের সময় নিয়ে স্বার্থপর হওয়ার অভিযোগ শুনতে হয়েছিল।”

দীর্ঘস্থায়ী অতিরিক্ত চাপ আবেগ ও মনের ক্ষতি করতে পারে

তীব্র, দীর্ঘস্থায়ী চাপ বা সমস্যা একা বহন করলে প্রচণ্ড মানসিক চাপ সৃষ্টি হতে পারে। সামান্য চাপ স্বাভাবিক, কিন্তু দীর্ঘস্থায়ী চাপ বিষণ্নতা, উদ্বেগ, হৃদ্‌রোগ এবং উচ্চ রক্তচাপ সৃষ্টি করতে পারে। দীর্ঘস্থায়ী চাপ আপনি কীভাবে সামলান, তা গুরুত্বপূর্ণ।

কখনো কখনো এই ধরনের অতিরিক্ত চাপের কথা সবাই জানে না। আমাদের সরল জীবনযাপনকারী খ্রিষ্টীয় সমাজে মর্মান্তিক ঘটনা ঘটলে সাধারণত প্রার্থনা, আর্থিক সহায়তা এবং সাপ্তাহিক বাজেটের হালনাগাদ তথ্য দেওয়া হয়। একই সময়ে, অন্য বিশ্বাসীরা আড়ালে গভীর কষ্ট ভোগ করছেন, অথচ তাঁদের কষ্টের স্বীকৃতি বা আর্থিক সাহায্য খুব কমই মেলে। এর কারণ হতে পারে টানাপোড়েনপূর্ণ সম্পর্ক, অথবা ছোট ছোট বিল জমে বড় অঙ্কের হয়ে ওঠা। বিশ্বাসঘাতকতা ও প্রত্যাখ্যান অপরিমেয় চাপ সৃষ্টি করে। পরিস্থিতির কারণে সৃষ্ট চাপের কোনো চটজলদি সমাধান নেই, কিন্তু আলোর ছোট ছোট ঝলক অন্ধকারে পথ খুঁজে পেতে আপনাকে সাহায্য করতে পারে।

আপনার পরিস্থিতি নিয়ে এমন কারও সঙ্গে কথা বলুন, যাঁকে আপনি বিশ্বাস করেন

কখনো কখনো শুধু সমস্যাগুলো নিয়ে কথা বলাই বিষয়গুলোকে সঠিক দৃষ্টিতে দেখতে সাহায্য করতে পারে। চাপের পরিস্থিতিটি নিজের মুখে প্রকাশ করতে শুনলে, কোনোভাবে মনের কুয়াশা কেটে যায় এবং সামনে এগোনোর পথ আরও স্পষ্ট হয়।

নিয়মিত দৈনন্দিন ছন্দ খুঁজে নিন

চাপ যখন প্রবল হয়ে ওঠে, তখন অনবরত ছুটে চলা চিন্তা, ভুলে যাওয়া এবং মনোযোগ দিতে না পারা অনাহূতভাবেই এসে পড়ে। দৈনন্দিন একটি নিয়ম অনুসরণ করলে আপনার মানসিক সুস্থতায় কিছুটা ছন্দ ফিরতে পারে। স্বাভাবিকতার সামান্যতম ছোঁয়াও এক মুহূর্তের আনন্দ এনে দেয় এবং প্রাণে প্রশান্তি আনে।

সচেতনভাবে একটু বিরতি খুঁজে নিন

দীর্ঘদিন ধরে থাকা চাপ অস্থিরতা, মেজাজের ওঠানামা এবং সবকিছু নিজের নিয়ন্ত্রণে নেওয়ার ইচ্ছা সৃষ্টি করতে পারে। কখনো কখনো মনের কুয়াশা পেরিয়ে চিন্তা করা কঠিন হয়, কিন্তু মানসিক সুস্থতার জন্য সতেজতা খুঁজে পাওয়া খুবই গুরুত্বপূর্ণ। চাপের হরমোন আপনার হৃদ্‌স্পন্দন বাড়িয়ে দিতে এবং রক্তনালিগুলো সংকুচিত করতে পারে। এতে সাময়িকভাবে আপনার রক্তচাপ বেড়ে যায়। আপনি শিথিল হলে এর বিপরীতটি ঘটে। শিথিল থাকলে মন আরও শান্ত ও স্পষ্ট হয়, যা আপনার মনোযোগ ও সিদ্ধান্ত নেওয়ার ক্ষমতা উন্নত করে।

বিশ্বাস করুন যে ঈশ্বর আপনার যত্ন নেন

কথাটি মুখে বলুন। বারবার গীতসংহিতা পড়ুন। ভালো সংগীত শুনুন। অল্প সময়ের জন্য হাঁটতে বেরোন এবং উচ্চস্বরে প্রার্থনা করুন। যীশুর দিকে দৃষ্টি রাখুন। বিশ্বাস করুন, “কান্না হয়তো এক রাত স্থায়ী হয়, কিন্তু সকালে আনন্দ আসে” (গীতসংহিতা 30:5)।

আপনি যদি পরিস্থিতির কারণে অতিরিক্ত চাপে পড়ে থাকেন, তবে ধৈর্যশীল ও বাস্তববাদী হোন। ঈশ্বর আপনার জন্য পথ করে দেবেন। অনেক সময়, আমাদের সামনে আর প্রায় কোনো উপায় না থাকলেই তিনি দরজা খুলে দেন। সেই ঘণ্টার জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় অনুগ্রহ তিনি জোগাবেন। আর পরের ঘণ্টার জন্যও। এবং তার পরেরটির জন্যও। কখনো কখনো অপ্রত্যাশিত সুযোগ আসে এবং অপ্রত্যাশিতভাবে প্রার্থনার উত্তর মেলে। আপনার জন্য তিনি যেভাবেই কাজ করার সিদ্ধান্ত নিন না কেন, তাঁর অপরিবর্তনীয় হাত ধরে থাকুন।

আপনি যে ধরনের অতিরিক্ত চাপেরই সম্মুখীন হোন না কেন, আপনার স্বর্গীয় পিতার দিকে ফিরুন।

তাঁর কাছে দিকনির্দেশনা ও প্রজ্ঞা চান। আর গীতরচকের সঙ্গে বলুন, “হে সদাপ্রভু, তোমাতেই আমি আস্থা রাখি; আমাকে কখনো লজ্জিত হতে দিয়ো না” (গীতসংহিতা 71:1)।

Eight-year-old Jamin wasn’t very smart. Or at least that’s what his older brother told him. Almost daily, brother Kenny found ways to remind Jamin of his shortcomings and laugh at his blunders.

“Jamin, you will never be smart”, Kenny said. Deep inside Jamin felt resigned to a life of muddled trip-ups. Would he always be clumsy? Would he always say things wrong? That’s what Kenny said.

Jamin believed Kenny’s lectures with wide-eyed belief. Kenny was three years older than him, so he must be right. Very well, then Jamin would be simple. Kenny would be smart. Life was not fair. Dad and Mom disliked Kenny’s proud talk and punished him whenever they walked in on one of his speeches. But Kenny had a way of avoiding earshot. So he continued mocking Jamin.

Grandma Otto watched these trials from her rocker on the porch. She was a quiet old lady.

“Jamin, do you know where Kenny is?” Mom asked with a smile. “It’s almost supper time.”

“He went to check his coyote traps. I’ll go find him.”

There was a chill in the air as he tramped up over the lawn, and the sun was growing old as he crossed the border of the woods. The fleeting shadows scurried over the hills. The chill deepened as he stumped further in. He breathed the rich air and followed Kenny’s trail. Eventually, the trail would end up in a meadow, but Jamin hoped he would find Kenny before he had to go that far. The various traps had been checked already, so Jamin knew Kenny had come this way. Jamin trudged on resolutely. His golden head caught the tired beams that fled from the sun as they flickered through the trees. And soon those too had faded leaving behind the musky smell of the woods. The fall webworms had been at work, and their web curtains shuttered from branches overhead.

At length, as the trees subdued and thinned, and the meadow appeared Jamin knew this was the end of his brother’s trap route. If Kenny wasn’t here, he wouldn’t know where else to look.

But Kenny was there. As Jamin clumped into the meadow, he could see a frustrated heap to his right. The heap’s voice had a familiar ring. The heap’s face was lit in pain. The heap was Kenny. “Are you alright? What happened?” Jamin felt strange, seeing Kenny scrunched in the dirt. Kenny was smart. “Did you step in a trap?”

“Yes, Jamin. I..I wasn’t looking where I was going. Help me. Please.”

Jamin bent and found an ankle firmly held in the jaws of a steel trap. Darkness stained the ground around Kenny. Quickly, Jamin’s strong arms pried open the jaws. Kenny reeled free. “Can you walk?”

“Yes. I think so. If you support me, I can hobble along.”

“Dad and Mom will be worried. We’ve missed supper.”

Sure enough, as the brothers hobbled back through the woods, they heard the long calling of their father. Jamin called back, and he was by their side in a moment, seeing the ankle and scooping up Kenny like a hurt sheep. The odd little band hurried home, and the screen door banged shut as Dad swept across the porch. Jamin went to the wash house and scrubbed his hands. He headed for the front door.

“Jamin.” It was Grandma. The porch light showed her in her old rocker. A heavy comforter lay on her shoulders.

“Yes, Grandma?”

“Do you think you are not very smart?”

“That’s what Kenny says.” Jamin squirmed.

“You were strong enough to open the trap, and Kenny wasn’t. You were brave enough to find him in the dark. Lots of young boys wouldn’t be.” Jamin was silent. Grandma Otto rocked some more, then smiled. “God made you the way you are for a reason, Jamin. He made Kenny the way he is for a reason. He has a plan for you, and a place only you can fill, you know.”

Jamin turned and walked into the warm kitchen. He was smiling.

ג'יימין בן השמונה לא היה חכם במיוחד. או לפחות כך אמר לו אחיו הגדול. כמעט מדי יום מצא אחיו קני דרכים להזכיר לג'יימין את חסרונותיו ולצחוק על הטעויות שלו.

״ג'יימין, אף פעם לא תהיה חכם״, אמר קני. עמוק בפנים השלים ג'יימין עם חיים של בלבול ומעידות. האם תמיד יהיה מגושם? האם תמיד יאמר דברים לא נכון? כך אמר קני.

ג'יימין האמין להטפותיו של קני באמון תמים. קני היה מבוגר ממנו בשלוש שנים, ולכן ודאי צדק. טוב, אם כך ג'יימין יהיה טיפש. קני יהיה חכם. החיים לא היו הוגנים. אבא ואמא לא אהבו את דבריו השחצניים של קני והענישו אותו בכל פעם שנכנסו באמצע אחד מנאומיו. אבל קני ידע איך לדבר בלי שישמעו אותו. וכך המשיך ללעוג לג'יימין.

סבתא אוטו צפתה בקשיים האלה מכיסא הנדנדה שלה במרפסת. היא הייתה אישה זקנה ושקטה.

״ג'יימין, אתה יודע איפה קני?״ שאלה אמא בחיוך. ״כמעט הגיע הזמן לארוחת הערב.״

״הוא הלך לבדוק את המלכודות שלו לזאבי ערבות. אלך למצוא אותו.״

קור הורגש באוויר כשצעד במעלה המדשאה, והשמש הלכה ושקעה כשחצה את גבול היער. הצללים החולפים התרוצצו על פני הגבעות. הקור גבר ככל שהתקדם פנימה בצעדים כבדים. הוא נשם את האוויר רווי הריחות והלך בעקבות קני. בסופו של דבר יוביל השביל לאחו, אבל ג'יימין קיווה למצוא את קני לפני שיצטרך להרחיק עד לשם. המלכודות השונות כבר נבדקו, ולכן ידע ג'יימין שקני עבר בדרך הזאת. ג'יימין המשיך לצעוד בנחישות. ראשו הזהוב קלט את הקרניים העייפות שנמלטו מן השמש וריצדו בין העצים. עד מהרה דעכו גם הן, והותירו אחריהן את ריחו המושקי של היער. זחלי העש הטווים קורים בסתיו כבר עשו את מלאכתם, ווילונות הקורים שלהם התנופפו מן הענפים שמעליו.

לבסוף, כשהעצים נעשו נמוכים ודלילים יותר והאחו התגלה לעיניו, ידע ג'יימין שזהו סוף מסלול המלכודות של אחיו. אם קני לא נמצא כאן, הוא לא ידע היכן עוד לחפש.

אבל קני היה שם. כשג'יימין נכנס לאחו בצעדים כבדים, ראה מימינו דמות מכווצת ומתוסכלת. קולה של הדמות נשמע מוכר. על פניה ניכר כאב. הדמות הייתה קני. ״אתה בסדר? מה קרה?״ ג'יימין הרגיש מוזר כשראה את קני מכווץ על האדמה. קני הרי היה חכם. ״דרכת בתוך מלכודת?״

״כן, ג'יימין. א..אני לא הסתכלתי לאן אני הולך. תעזור לי. בבקשה.״

ג'יימין התכופף ומצא קרסול לכוד בחוזקה בין הלסתות של מלכודת פלדה. כתם כהה כיסה את האדמה סביב קני. במהירות פתח ג'יימין בכוח זרועותיו החזקות את הלסתות. קני נחלץ והתנודד. ״אתה יכול ללכת?״

״כן. נראה לי שכן. אם תתמוך בי, אוכל להתקדם בצליעה.״

״אבא ואמא ידאגו. החמצנו את ארוחת הערב.״

ואכן, כשהאחים עשו את דרכם בחזרה דרך היער בצליעה, שמעו את קריאתו הממושכת של אביהם. ג'יימין קרא אליו בחזרה, ובתוך רגע היה אבא לצדם. הוא ראה את הקרסול והרים את קני בזרועותיו כמו כבשה פצועה. החבורה הקטנה והמוזרה מיהרה הביתה, ודלת הרשת נטרקה כשאבא חצה במהירות את המרפסת. ג'יימין הלך למבנה הרחצה וקרצף את ידיו. הוא פנה אל דלת הכניסה.

״ג'יימין.״ זאת הייתה סבתא. אור המרפסת האיר אותה בכיסא הנדנדה הישן שלה. שמיכת פוך כבדה הייתה מונחת על כתפיה.

״כן, סבתא?״

״אתה חושב שאתה לא חכם במיוחד?״

״זה מה שקני אומר.״ ג'יימין התפתל באי־נוחות.

״היית חזק מספיק כדי לפתוח את המלכודת, וקני לא היה. היית אמיץ מספיק כדי למצוא אותו בחושך. הרבה ילדים בגילך לא היו מעזים.״ ג'יימין שתק. סבתא אוטו התנדנדה עוד קצת, ואז חייכה. ״אלוהים ברא אותך כפי שאתה מסיבה מסוימת, ג'יימין. הוא ברא את קני כפי שהוא מסיבה מסוימת. יש לו תוכנית בשבילך, ומקום שרק אתה יכול למלא, אתה יודע.״

ג'יימין הסתובב ונכנס למטבח החמים. הוא חייך.

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Hvor utrolig er det ikke at Gud kan ta en elendig synder uten frykt for Herren og gjøre ham til en hellig, renset i blodet, og en forkynner av evangeliet! I denne fortellingen ser vi Guds livsforvandlende kraft i virksomhet i salmedikterens liv.

På den lille kirkegården i Olney i England står en gravstein av granitt med denne innskriften, skrevet av Newton selv før hans død:

John Newton, en gang en vantro og en utsvevende mann, en tjener for slaver i Afrika, ble ved vår Herre og Frelser Jesu Kristi rike barmhjertighet bevart, gjenopprettet, tilgitt og utpekt til å forkynne den troen han lenge hadde arbeidet for å ødelegge!

Denne gravskriften beskriver treffende det uvanlige og fargerike livet til denne mannen, en av de store evangeliske forkynnerne på 1700-tallet. Hans vitnesbyrd var: «Ved Guds nåde er jeg det jeg er!»

«Amazing Grace» er en salme som ble utgitt i 1779, med tekst skrevet i 1772 av den engelske dikteren og anglikanske presten John Newton (1725–1807). «Amazing Grace» er sannsynligvis den mest elskede salmen fra de siste to århundrene. Det anslås at denne salmen fremføres 10 millioner ganger i året. Den har vært med på over 11 000 album og er oversatt til omtrent 60 språk. Den ble omtalt i Harriet Beecher Stowes roman mot slaveriet, Onkel Toms hytte. Populariteten steg kraftig under to av Amerikas største kriser: borgerkrigen og Vietnamkrigen.

Ironisk nok ble denne gripende sangen, som er nært knyttet til det afroamerikanske samfunnet, skrevet av en tidligere slavehandler, John Newton.

John ble født 24. juli 1725 i Wapping i England. Faren, John Newton, Sr., var sjømann, og moren, Elizabeth Newton, var en hengiven kristen. Faren elsket ham, men var til sjøs det meste av tiden. Moren var derimot øm og omsorgsfull og lærte ham Guds ord. Hun lærte ham å huske hele kapitler fra Bibelen utenat og tok ham med i kirken. Dessverre døde moren av tuberkulose da han var nesten sju år gammel. Faren giftet seg igjen kort tid senere og sendte ham på internatskole. Mens han var der, fikk han dårlige venner. Karakteren hans forfalt så mye at han ble utvist fra én skole og flyttet til en annen. Da han var blitt 11 år, ville ikke internatskolene ha ham, så faren tok ham med til sjøs. De neste seks årene tilbrakte han på Atlanterhavet sammen med faren.

Da John var 17 år, ordnet faren det slik at han skulle reise til Jamaica for å få en godt betalt stilling som oppsynsmann på en plantasje. Underveis, mens han ventet på at skipet skulle gå, ble John invitert hjem til noen gamle venner, familien Catlett. Det var i dette hjemmet moren til John hadde dødd ti år tidligere. Da han fornyet bekjentskapet med dem, ble han kjent med datteren deres, Mary. Mødrene til John og Mary hadde vært bestevenninner. John var invitert til å bli i fire dager, men han ble i to uker og gikk glipp av skipet til Jamaica.

Som 18-åring ble John tvangsinnrullert i den britiske marinen, og livet hans gikk fra vondt til verre. Han ville dra tilbake for å se Mary, så han deserterte fra skipet, men ble tatt, pisket offentlig og lagt i jern. Livet hans om bord var så ugudelig at selv de andre gudløse sjøfolkene krympet seg ved hans banning og gudsbespottelser. Han fikk tilnavnet «Den store gudsbespotteren» og var så uønsket om bord at han ble sendt for å arbeide på et slaveskip.

En av eierne av slaveskipet der han nå arbeidet, tilbød John en jobb når de kom til Afrikas kyst. Men straks han kom i land, ble han bundet og tvunget til å arbeide med lite mat, klær eller husly. I denne tiden sendte han flere brev hjem til faren og bønnfalt ham om hjelp.

Et skip som het The Greyhound, seilte nær kysten som John nå kalte sitt hjem. Kapteinen hadde fått beskjed av Johns far om å lete etter sønnen hans. Selv om skipet var nesten for langt fra land til å drive handel, bestemte de seg for å gjøre et forsøk. En venn av John rodde ut fra land for å handle. Da han snudde seg for å dra, spurte kapteinen om han kjente noen som het John Newton. Til kapteinens overraskelse gjorde han det, og John ble hentet om bord for å reise hjem.

Om bord tok Newton opp et eksemplar av Thomas á Kempis’ kristne klassiker, Om Kristi etterfølgelse. Han hadde aldri møtt noe lignende, og han begynte å undre seg over om det kristendommen hevdet, kunne være sant. Den natten, 10. mars 1748, var en voldsom storm nær ved å senke skipet. Menn, dyr og proviant ble skylt over bord. Stormen vekket Newton; bølgene hadde knust skipets råtne treverk, og vann strømmet virvlende inn i lugaren hans. John ba for første gang på mange år.

The Greyhound ble kastet omkring i stormen i Nord-Atlanteren i over 11 dager. Med lite håp om å overleve arbeidet sjøfolkene mekanisk ved pumpene og prøvde å holde fartøyet flytende. På stormens ellevte dag var John for utmattet til å pumpe, så han ble bundet til roret, der han gjorde sitt beste for å holde skipet på kurs. Fra klokken ett til midnatt sto han ved roret. Han fryktet at han kom til å dø, og at hvis den kristne troen var sann, ville han helt sikkert ikke bli tilgitt. Han tenkte over alt han hadde gjort de siste årene. Livet hans virket like ødelagt og havarert som det medtatte skipet han forsøkte å styre gjennom stormen. I disse lange og utmattende timene ropte Newton til Gud som aldri før, og det ble vendepunktet i livet hans.

Det var en dag John Newton husket resten av livet. «På den dagen sendte Herren hjelp fra det høye og reddet meg ut av dype vann.» Over 50 år senere, 21. mars 1805, skrev John i dagboken sin: «Jeg makter ikke å skrive særlig godt; men jeg prøver å markere denne dagen når den kommer igjen, med ydmykelse, bønn og lovprisning.»

Bare Guds forunderlige nåde kunne ta en rå, gudsbespottende sjømann som drev slavehandel, og forvandle ham til et Guds barn. John sluttet aldri å undre seg over Guds verk i livet hans. Han fikk interesse for bønn, for å lese og grunne på Skriften og for bare å tale ord som var til behag for Gud.

Da han kom hjem, så Mary og foreldrene hennes den forandringen Herren hadde gjort i John. De to giftet seg 1. februar 1750.

De neste fire årene var Newton kaptein på sitt eget slaveskip. Dette arbeidet holdt ham borte fra Mary i flere måneder om gangen. Mens de var fra hverandre, brevvekslet de stadig. I brevene skrev John gjentatte ganger om hvordan kjærligheten og ekteskapet deres økte hans takknemlighet overfor Herren. «... Når jeg tillater meg å dvele særlig ved tanken på deg, fører det meg vanligvis videre og får meg ned på kne for å velsigne Herren for at han har gitt meg en slik skatt, og for å be om din fred og ditt vel.»

John forsøkte å «kristne» slaveskipet sitt ved å holde søndagsgudstjenester for besetningen på 30 menn som var forherdet av synd. Han foretok ytterligere tre reiser for å føre slaver fra Afrika til Nord-Amerika. Mens han planla sin fjerde reise, ble han syk av malaria. Gud brukte denne sykdommen til å avslutte hans deltakelse i slavehandelen.

Da John begynte på et nytt kapittel i livet, følte han seg kalt til å bli prest. I mer enn 50 år forkynte han evangeliet og var en av de mest innflytelsesrike mennene i sin tid.

John Newton skrev ofte en salme til kveldsgudstjenestene sine på søndager. I 1779 ble 280 av disse samlet sammen med 68 salmer av Newtons venn og sognebarn William Cowper og utgitt som Olney Hymns. Den mest kjente av alle salmene i Olney Hymns, «Troens tilbakeblikk og forventning», sprang ut av Davids utrop i 1. Krønikebok 17:16-17. I dag kjenner vi den som «Amazing Grace». «Amazing Grace» hadde opprinnelig seks strofer, og det siste verset ble lagt til omtrent et århundre senere. De fleste salmebøker har fire eller fem av disse versene.

Som prest i kirken ble John stadig mer plaget av slavehandelen som fremdeles pågikk. I 1788, 34 år etter at han hadde forlatt slavehandelen, skrev han en bok med tittelen Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade og sendte den til alle parlamentsmedlemmene. Denne boken gjorde offentligheten oppmerksom på slavehandelens onder. Han sier dette: «Det sier seg selv at det å fange, selge og frakte svarte slaver til plantasjene i Vestindia og Amerika var en grusom og ondartet levemåte.» Med Guds hjelp og forsyn fikk John oppleve den dagen i 1807, noen måneder før sin død, da slaveriet offisielt ble forbudt i England.

Da John var i sekstiårene, døde hans elskede kone Mary. Dette var en stor prøvelse for John, og han tilbrakte de siste 17 årene av livet uten henne.

Etter at John hadde fått slag, og kort tid før hans død, oppfordret en talsmann for kirken Newton til å vurdere å slutte å forkynne på grunn av sviktende helse, syn og hukommelse. John svarte: «Hva, skal den gamle gudsbespotteren fra Afrika slutte mens han ennå kan snakke? Jeg vil fortsette å forkynne. Selv om hukommelsen min svikter, husker jeg to ting svært tydelig: Jeg er en stor synder, og Kristus er en stor Frelser.»

John Newtons siste ord da han lå på dødsleiet, var disse: «Jeg er fremdeles i de døendes land; snart skal jeg være i de levendes land.»

Melodien til «Amazing Grace» er en tidlig amerikansk folkemelodi. Den var først kjent som en plantasjemelodi med tittelen «Loving Lambs». Denne melodien ble først utgitt i 1831 i boken The Virginia Harmony. De fleste salmebøker som ble utgitt etter dette, tok med denne sangen. I 1910 la Edwin O. Excell til det siste verset, som etter hvert erstattet sangens tre siste opprinnelige vers. Hans utgave av sangen er den vanligste i salmebøkene våre i dag. Flere andre av Newtons Olney-salmer synges fortsatt i dag, blant annet «Hvor liflig Jesu navn lyder» og «Herlighet tales om deg».

“Dr. Waldron, Elsie needs help!” Elsie’s husband was adamant, almost angry, as he stared at me. On the other hand, Elsie stared at the floor, almost as though she wasn’t present. I had never met either of the couple before and was struggling just a little to figure out what was needed from me to help her.

“What is going on?” I asked as I flipped through her chart. This was still in the days of paper charts, and I headed to the lab section of her chart. There wasn’t anything too crazy that I could see there—her liver enzymes were a little elevated, but otherwise, everything seemed OK.

“It’s her drinking!” Her husband told me. “She is drinking more and more every night. She won’t go out except to get whiskey. She drinks till she passes out every night and has to have something every morning to get her started.”

“Is that true?” I asked Elsie, feeling like a judge overseeing a jury trial.

“Yes,” she said. Her face was emotionless, and I couldn’t tell if she wanted to be there or not.

“Do you want help?” I asked her. This was a loaded question. Many people who struggle with alcoholism aren’t ready to break free from its vice-like hold on them. Maybe Elsie was different.

“I guess so,” she said, indifferently. Once again, I couldn’t tell whether she wanted to be there or not.

“At the rate at which you are drinking, you will kill yourself within a year – maybe two at best – if you don’t give up alcohol entirely,” I told her. “If you want to, I will try to find you an inpatient program to detox you and get you off of alcohol.”

“She’s ready,” he husband said firmly.

When dealing with someone who drinks heavily, it is crucial that they don’t simply stop drinking without medical support. Abrupt cessation of alcohol use causes the body to go into withdrawal which can produce a state called Delirium Tremens and even seizures.

I stepped out of the exam room and to make phone calls. It is never easy to find a place for someone to attempt to rehabilitate from any kind of substances, and it was over an hour and a half before I found a facility that was willing to take Elsie and try to help her get off of the whiskey.

I sighed as I reentered her exam room. I had been afraid that I wouldn’t find anywhere for her to go.

I told them about the plan, and her husband nodded vigorously, while Elise continued to stare silently at the floor. “Can we pray together before you go?” I asked them, and when they nodded assent, I prayed with them, asking for freedom and Jesus’ presence in both of their lives.

They left my office with marching orders and directions on where to go. I had a happy glow about me for the rest of the morning, knowing that I had gone the extra mile and had really made a difference in this middle-aged couple’s life.

Around 2 pm, I got a call from the rehab facility. They hadn’t seen even a shadow of Elsie or her husband, which was surprising, since it was a bright sunny day and the facility wasn’t that far away. With a sinking feeling, I dialed the couple’s phone number.

“She won’t go!” Her husband told me. “She tells me that she told me this ahead of time. She’ll try to cut back, but she isn’t willing to go into a rehab facility or any such thing. I guess just tell them that we’ll let them know if she changes her mind.”

My nurse called the rehab facility and told them the bad news, and I sat down in my chair, stunned. What else could I have done? Was there a solution for Elsie—something different that I could have said that would have made a difference in her life?

About a year later, I received the sad news that Elsie had died at home. I was certain that things would have been different if she had gone to rehab and if she had given control to Jesus. None of that had happened, and I felt cynicism pushing into my heart.

Cynicism

We live in an age of cynicism. In ancient Greece, the cynics were an odd assortment of men who specialized in being grouchy and saying mean (they would have said truthful) things to people. They often dressed in rags and behaved in such a way that most of the polite Athenians did not want to be close to them.

Today, cynicism means a tendency to believe the worst about people and circumstances. Cynical people believe that all people are motivated purely by selfishness and that bad events will tend to prevail.

Many young doctors are idealistic and very hopeful. They believe that if they exert the utmost effort, they can make a real, positive impact on their patient’s lives. Unfortunately, as time goes by and they try their hardest and their patients don’t change, they can give up. These doctors still try, but they no longer really hope that their efforts will make much of a difference.

It seems as though people who get involved with politics often have the best of intentions. They see this as a path to changing society for the better. Unfortunately, as time goes by and the faces in charge change, the policies don’t really change, they tend to become cynical.

Sometimes this cynicism is directed against all politicians. Sometimes it is only anger directed against members of the party that opposes their party’s positions. Hope is replaced by cynicism.

Cynicism in the Bible

If there is a book in the Bible that seems to have been written by a cynical man, it is the book of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who we understand to be Solomon, lists all of the things that he endeavored in an attempt to find joy.

In chapter 2:17-23 Solomon describes work as futile. He finishes by saying, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

He saw the world as being dominated by tyrants and there was little that the people could do about it. Solomon went so far as to say that political power was meaningless “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiastes 6:6, he seems to disparage long life. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Of course, he finishes his short book with the instruction to remember our Creator in the days of our youth. There is a blessing for those who choose to focus on God when they have a little bit of energy left and not, when they are old and jaded, like Solomon.

Later on, it almost seemed as though God had given up on His people. He still sent prophets to them, but He knew without a doubt that the people would refuse to respond. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Even in the New Testament, Paul told Timothy that the time was coming when people would no longer listen to sound doctrine. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

By picking and choosing these passages, we can come away with a very gloomy view of the future and, more specifically, of human’s willingness to change. It seems there is little point of investing ourselves in the people around us. They are full of woe and are as likely to change as a chipmunk is to master differential calculus.

The Opposite of Cynicism

The opposite of cynicism is hope. It is the belief that the future could be better.

It is interesting that the Apostle Paul spoke of tribulations in the Epistle to the Romans, “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

We may not have reached the place where we glory in the trials we experience, but certainly, they should bring us these other things that he mentions. For, we grow in patience and experience, even as we deal with trials, but more than that, we come to realize that we have hope for tomorrow because we serve a great God.

The contrast in the story of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15 teaches us much about hope. The father and the older brother were strikingly different in their attitudes.

The father had never given up hope – he knew that his son had failed him and gone far from what he knew was right and yet, the father still desired to see the prodigal come to himself and return home.

On the other hand, the older brother not only had no hope for his younger brother, but he was also angry with him. The prodigal had wasted his money, he had lived in sin, and now, he had returned home just because he was out of money.

Certainly, there was no reason to trust the younger son. Yet, that is exactly what our Heavenly Father does for us.

Look for Hope in the Right Places

Part of the problem is that we look for hope in the wrong places. A number of years ago, a presidential candidate ran for office under the slogan “Hope and Change,” and yet, even though he was elected, I imagine most folks did not feel that their lives were significantly changed for the better.

Pursuing the things this world values—political power and wealth is guaranteed to bring emptiness. This is Satan’s pattern—he always over-promises and under-delivers.

This was what he did when he tempted Jesus, “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). All of the things Satan offered, nothing compared with the glory that Jesus eventually received from the road that led to the cross.

In the same way, Satan would like to distract Christians from seeking the things that are valuable, and that will bring hope. Satan tells Christians that politics will not only change the world for the better, it is an easier way to change the world.

The Bible is clear that we build hope as we nurture our relationship with God and then work to help our brothers and sisters build that same relationship in their own lives. The reason that we can hope is not because people are so wonderful—we don’t have to live very long to realize that they aren’t. The reason we hope is because we serve an awesome, faithful God who walks with us through the worst of our trials.

Remember that We Have Undeserved Hope

Jesus’ messages about forgiveness make it clear that one of the major reasons that we have for forgiving others in our lives is that we have received great and undeserved forgiveness. The same is true for hope.

Each one of us was hopeless and without reason to expect to receive hope and we were still given a ray of light in the midst of our darkness. Maybe part of the reason that we have so much trouble hoping for good things for the people around us is that we do not remember how hopeless we were before we found grace.

If Jesus was able to bring hope to our hopeless existence, then certainly He can do wonderful things in the hearts and lives of others around us. The only people we should give up on are the ones that our Savior has given up on as well.

Small Efforts Do Make a Difference

I remember having a conversation with a young person who was planning to go into medicine and had a plan to go to a foreign country and serve the people there. As we were talking, an older man entered the conversation and shared that he saw little hope for change in developing countries.

The people in those countries just weren’t interested in getting better and didn’t do the minimum necessary to stave off things like worms and parasites. Doctors and nurses couldn’t make a difference in such an environment.

I could sense the heart of the youth sinking as this older man shared. He had experience, and he had given up hope. The sad thing was that he was also stealing the hope of someone who still had a desire to serve.

When I was in training, I had a surgeon tell me that family doctors didn’t really do anything. They simply kept their patients alive till their next office visit, whereas surgeons really “fixed” people—taking out (or off) the offending body part.

At the end of the day, small efforts do make a difference. I don’t do brain surgery, but I still can make a difference in someone else’s life— maybe just by spending a little time and listening and praying. This is true for all of us.

More than that, we come to realize that making this effort changes our own lives for the better. Jesus told the sheep that as they ministered to “the least of these my brethren,” they were ministering to Him.

Even if no one’s life is improved, our Savior knows our desires and feels our efforts, and will reward them someday.

A Few Things to Remember

When we face failures, we tend to move in one of two directions. Those of us who are optimists tend to believe that this episode was an isolated event and that the future is still bright. On the other hand, pessimists believe that failures are permanent, personal, and pervasive.

Pessimists believe that their failures are the result of intrinsic character flaws that they have and that these things affect all of their lives and are unlikely to change. Unlike the righteous man who falls to rise again, these people fall and lie where they fall, defeated at the outset.

When we are dealing with other people, we need to give them the same grace that we should give ourselves. They, too, are growing, and if they have a failure today, they will do better tomorrow. Maybe they will fail again, but they will at least “fail better.”

Conclusion

Cynicism is rife in our world. Many have given up hope for a better future, and it is understandable for those who have invested their hope in this world’s institutions. There is no real hope in government or in armies or in bureaucracy.

The song says, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” For, Jesus is the one who brings light into our darkness and allows us to continue, even when others fail us.

God is the one who redeems us. He is the one who sent the prophets, even though their messages were ignored, and the prophets were persecuted. He is the one who continues to hope for us, even when we have failed Him so many times in the past.

He is the reason we carry on. He is the reason that we have hope, not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.

“Dkt. Waldron, Elsie anahitaji msaada!” Mume wa Elsie alisisitiza kwa uthabiti, karibu kwa hasira, huku akinitazama kwa makini. Kwa upande mwingine, Elsie aliutazama sakafu, karibu kana kwamba hakuwepo pale. Sikuwa nimekutana na yeyote kati yao hapo awali, na nilikuwa nikihangaika kidogo kuelewa nilichopaswa kufanya ili kumsaidia.

“Kuna nini?” niliuliza huku nikipitia jalada lake la matibabu. Hizo zilikuwa bado siku za kutumia majalada ya karatasi, nami nikaenda kwenye sehemu ya vipimo vya maabara. Sikuona jambo lolote lisilo la kawaida sana humo—viwango vya vimeng'enya vya ini lake vilikuwa vimepanda kidogo, lakini mbali na hilo, kila kitu kilionekana kuwa sawa.

“Ni unywaji wake wa pombe!” mumewe aliniambia. “Anakunywa zaidi na zaidi kila usiku. Hatoki nje isipokuwa kwenda kununua whisky. Anakunywa mpaka anapoteza fahamu kila usiku, na lazima anywe pombe kila asubuhi ili aweze kuanza shughuli zake.”

“Hilo ni kweli?” nilimuuliza Elsie, nikihisi kama hakimu anayesimamia kesi mbele ya baraza la waamuzi.

“Ndiyo,” alisema. Uso wake haukuonyesha hisia zozote, nami sikuweza kujua kama alitaka kuwa pale au la.

“Unataka msaada?” nilimuuliza. Hili lilikuwa swali lenye uzito mkubwa. Watu wengi wanaopambana na uraibu wa pombe hawako tayari kujinasua kutoka katika mtego wake unaowabana kwa nguvu. Huenda Elsie alikuwa tofauti.

“Nadhani hivyo,” alisema bila kujali. Kwa mara nyingine, sikuweza kujua kama alitaka kuwa pale au la.

“Kwa kiwango hiki cha unywaji wako, utajiua ndani ya mwaka mmoja—au miaka miwili kwa hali nzuri zaidi—usipoacha pombe kabisa,” nilimwambia. “Ukitaka, nitajaribu kukutafutia mpango wa matibabu ya kulazwa ili kuondoa utegemezi wa pombe mwilini mwako na kukusaidia kuiacha.”

“Yuko tayari,” mumewe alisema kwa uthabiti.

Unapomhudumia mtu anayekunywa pombe kupita kiasi, ni muhimu sana kwamba asiache tu kunywa bila msaada wa kitabibu. Kuacha kutumia pombe ghafla husababisha mwili kupata dalili za kuacha pombe, ambazo zinaweza kuleta hali inayoitwa Delirium Tremens na hata degedege.

Nilitoka katika chumba cha uchunguzi ili kupiga simu. Si rahisi kamwe kupata mahali ambapo mtu anaweza kujaribu kupata matibabu ya kuachana na aina yoyote ya dawa au vilevi, na ilichukua zaidi ya saa moja na nusu kabla sijapata kituo kilichokuwa tayari kumpokea Elsie na kujaribu kumsaidia kuacha whisky.

Nilishusha pumzi nilipoingia tena katika chumba chake cha uchunguzi. Nilikuwa nimehofia kwamba nisingepata mahali popote ambapo angeweza kwenda.

Niliwaeleza mpango huo, na mumewe akatikisa kichwa kwa nguvu kukubali, huku Elise akiendelea kuitazama sakafu kimya kimya. “Tunaweza kuomba pamoja kabla hamjaondoka?” niliwauliza, na walipokubali kwa kutikisa vichwa, niliomba pamoja nao, nikiomba uhuru na uwepo wa Yesu katika maisha yao wote wawili.

Waliondoka ofisini kwangu wakiwa na maagizo ya kufanya na maelekezo ya mahali pa kwenda. Nilijawa na furaha kwa muda wote uliobaki wa asubuhi hiyo, nikijua kwamba nilikuwa nimejitahidi zaidi ya ilivyotarajiwa na kweli nilikuwa nimeleta mabadiliko katika maisha ya wanandoa hawa wa makamo.

Karibu saa 14:00, nilipigiwa simu kutoka kituo cha matibabu ya uraibu. Hawakuwa wamemwona hata kwa mbali Elsie wala mumewe, jambo lililoshangaza, kwani ilikuwa siku yenye jua kali na kituo hicho hakikuwa mbali sana. Huku nikianza kuvunjika moyo, nilipiga namba ya simu ya wanandoa hao.

“Hataki kwenda!” mumewe aliniambia. “Ananiambia kwamba alikuwa ameniambia jambo hili mapema. Atajaribu kupunguza unywaji, lakini hayuko tayari kwenda katika kituo cha matibabu ya uraibu au mahali popote kama hapo. Nadhani waambie tu kwamba tutawajulisha akibadili mawazo.”

Muuguzi wangu alipiga simu kwenye kituo cha matibabu ya uraibu na kuwaeleza habari hizo mbaya, nami nikaketi kwenye kiti changu, nikiwa nimepigwa na butwaa. Ningefanya nini kingine? Je, kulikuwa na suluhisho kwa Elsie—jambo tofauti ambalo ningesema na ambalo lingeleta mabadiliko katika maisha yake?

Karibu mwaka mmoja baadaye, nilipokea habari za kusikitisha kwamba Elsie alikuwa amefariki nyumbani. Nilikuwa na hakika kwamba mambo yangekuwa tofauti kama angeenda kwenye matibabu ya uraibu na kama angemkabidhi Yesu uongozi wa maisha yake. Hakuna kati ya hayo lililotokea, nami nikahisi mtazamo wa kutarajia mabaya ukiingia moyoni mwangu.

Mtazamo wa Kutarajia Mabaya

Tunaishi katika enzi ya mtazamo wa kutarajia mabaya. Katika Ugiriki ya kale, wafuasi wa falsafa ya Kisiniki walikuwa kundi lisilo la kawaida la wanaume waliobobea katika kununa na kuwaambia watu maneno yenye ukali (wao wangesema yenye ukweli). Mara nyingi walivaa matambara na kutenda kwa namna ambayo iliwafanya Waathene wengi wenye adabu wasitake kuwa karibu nao.

Leo, mtazamo huo unamaanisha mwelekeo wa kuamini mambo mabaya zaidi kuhusu watu na hali mbalimbali. Watu wenye mtazamo huo wanaamini kwamba watu wote husukumwa na ubinafsi pekee na kwamba mambo mabaya ndiyo yatakayotawala.

Madaktari wengi vijana wana malengo bora na matumaini makubwa sana. Wanaamini kwamba wakijitahidi kwa kadiri wawezavyo, wanaweza kuleta mabadiliko halisi na mazuri katika maisha ya wagonjwa wao. Kwa bahati mbaya, kadiri muda unavyopita na wanavyojitahidi sana bila wagonjwa wao kubadilika, wanaweza kukata tamaa. Madaktari hawa bado hujaribu, lakini hawana tena matumaini ya kweli kwamba juhudi zao zitaleta mabadiliko makubwa.

Inaonekana kwamba watu wanaojihusisha na siasa mara nyingi huwa na nia njema kabisa. Wanaona siasa kama njia ya kuibadilisha jamii iwe bora. Kwa bahati mbaya, kadiri muda unavyopita na watu walio madarakani wanavyobadilika, bila sera kubadilika kweli, wao huelekea kuwa na mtazamo wa kutarajia mabaya.

Wakati mwingine mtazamo huu huelekezwa dhidi ya wanasiasa wote. Wakati mwingine ni hasira tu inayoelekezwa dhidi ya wanachama wa chama kinachopinga misimamo ya chama chao. Matumaini hubadilishwa na mtazamo wa kutarajia mabaya.

Mtazamo wa Kutarajia Mabaya katika Biblia

Ikiwa kuna kitabu katika Biblia kinachoonekana kuandikwa na mtu mwenye mtazamo wa kutarajia mabaya, ni kitabu cha Mhubiri. Mhubiri, ambaye tunaelewa kuwa ni Sulemani, anaorodhesha mambo yote aliyojitahidi kufanya akitafuta furaha.

Katika sura ya 2:17-23 Sulemani anaeleza kazi kuwa haina faida. Anamalizia kwa kusema, “Kwa maana mwanadamu anapata nini kutokana na kazi yake yote na fadhaa ya moyo wake, ambayo kwayo ametaabika chini ya jua? Kwa maana siku zake zote ni huzuni, na taabu yake ni majonzi; naam, hata usiku moyo wake haupumziki. Hili nalo ni ubatili.” (Mhubiri 2:22,23)

Aliuona ulimwengu kuwa umetawaliwa na watawala dhalimu, na watu hawakuwa na mengi ya kufanya kuhusu hilo. Sulemani alifikia hata kusema kwamba mamlaka ya kisiasa hayakuwa na maana: “Afadhali mtoto maskini mwenye hekima kuliko mfalme mzee mpumbavu asiyekubali tena kuonywa. Kwa maana anatoka gerezani ili kutawala; hali kadhalika aliyezaliwa katika ufalme wake huwa maskini” (Mhubiri 4:13).

Katika Mhubiri 6:6, anaonekana kudharau maisha marefu. “Naam, hata akiishi miaka elfu mara mbili, lakini hajaona mema: je, wote hawaendi mahali pamoja?”

Bila shaka, anamalizia kitabu chake kifupi kwa agizo la kumkumbuka Muumba wetu katika siku za ujana wetu. Kuna baraka kwa wale wanaochagua kumwelekezea Mungu fikira zao wakati wangali na nguvu kidogo, wala si wanapokuwa wazee na wamechoshwa na maisha, kama Sulemani.

Baadaye, karibu ilionekana kana kwamba Mungu alikuwa amekata tamaa kuhusu watu Wake. Bado aliwatumia manabii, lakini alijua bila shaka kwamba watu wangekataa kuitikia. “Kwa hiyo utawaambia maneno haya yote; lakini hawatakusikiliza; utawaita pia, lakini hawatakujibu” (Yeremia 7:27).

Hata katika Agano Jipya, Paulo alimwambia Timotheo kwamba wakati ulikuwa unakuja ambapo watu hawangesikiliza tena mafundisho sahihi. “Kwa maana wakati utakuja ambapo hawatayavumilia mafundisho sahihi; bali kwa kufuata tamaa zao wenyewe watajikusanyia walimu, kwa kuwa masikio yao yanawasha kusikia wanachokitaka;” (2 Timotheo 4:3).

Kwa kuchagua vifungu hivi pekee, tunaweza kuondoka tukiwa na mtazamo wa huzuni sana kuhusu wakati ujao na, hasa, kuhusu utayari wa wanadamu kubadilika. Inaonekana kuna faida ndogo sana katika kujitoa kwa ajili ya watu wanaotuzunguka. Wamejaa taabu, na uwezekano wao wa kubadilika ni sawa na uwezekano wa kindi wa aina ya chipmunk kuimudu kalkulasi ya diferenshali.

Kinyume cha Mtazamo wa Kutarajia Mabaya

Kinyume cha mtazamo wa kutarajia mabaya ni matumaini. Ni imani kwamba wakati ujao unaweza kuwa bora.

Inavutia kwamba Mtume Paulo alizungumza kuhusu dhiki katika Waraka kwa Warumi, “Wala si hivyo tu, bali tunajivunia pia dhiki: tukijua kwamba dhiki huleta saburi; na saburi, uzoefu; na uzoefu, matumaini; na matumaini hayatuaibishi; kwa sababu upendo wa Mungu umemiminwa mioyoni mwetu kwa Roho Mtakatifu tuliyepewa” (Warumi 5:3-5).

Huenda hatujafikia hatua ya kujivunia majaribu tunayopitia, lakini kwa hakika yanapaswa kutuletea mambo hayo mengine anayoyataja. Kwa maana tunakua katika saburi na uzoefu, hata tunapokabiliana na majaribu, lakini zaidi ya hayo, tunatambua kwamba tuna matumaini kwa ajili ya kesho kwa sababu tunamtumikia Mungu mkuu.

Tofauti iliyopo katika simulizi la Mwana Mpotevu katika Luka 15 inatufundisha mengi kuhusu matumaini. Baba na kaka mkubwa walitofautiana sana katika mitazamo yao.

Baba hakuwahi kukata tamaa—alijua kwamba mwanawe alikuwa amemwangusha na kwenda mbali na kile alichojua kuwa sahihi, lakini bado baba alitamani kumwona mwana mpotevu akirudiwa na fahamu na kurudi nyumbani.

Kwa upande mwingine, kaka mkubwa hakuwa tu hana matumaini kuhusu mdogo wake, bali pia alimkasirikia. Mwana mpotevu alikuwa ametapanya fedha zake, alikuwa ameishi katika dhambi, na sasa alikuwa amerudi nyumbani kwa sababu tu alikuwa ameishiwa fedha.

Kwa hakika, hakukuwa na sababu ya kumwamini mwana mdogo. Hata hivyo, hicho ndicho hasa Baba yetu wa Mbinguni anachotufanyia.

Tafuta Matumaini Mahali Panapofaa

Sehemu ya tatizo ni kwamba tunatafuta matumaini mahali pasipofaa. Miaka kadhaa iliyopita, mgombea wa urais aligombea kwa kaulimbiu “Matumaini na Mabadiliko,” lakini hata ingawa alichaguliwa, ninadhani watu wengi hawakuhisi kwamba maisha yao yalikuwa yamebadilika kwa kiasi kikubwa na kuwa bora.

Kufuatilia vitu ambavyo ulimwengu huu unavithamini—mamlaka ya kisiasa na utajiri—bila shaka huleta utupu. Hii ndiyo njia ya Shetani—daima huahidi mengi kuliko anavyotimiza.

Hicho ndicho alichofanya alipomjaribu Yesu, “Nitakupa vitu hivi vyote, ukianguka chini na kuniabudu” (Mathayo 4:8). Kati ya vitu vyote ambavyo Shetani alitoa, hakuna kilicholingana na utukufu ambao Yesu alipokea hatimaye kupitia njia iliyoelekea msalabani.

Vivyo hivyo, Shetani angependa kuwavuruga Wakristo wasitafute vitu vyenye thamani ambavyo vitaleta matumaini. Shetani huwaambia Wakristo kwamba siasa hazitaubadilisha tu ulimwengu uwe bora, bali pia ni njia rahisi zaidi ya kuubadilisha ulimwengu.

Biblia inaweka wazi kwamba tunajenga matumaini tunapoulea uhusiano wetu na Mungu na kisha kufanya kazi kuwasaidia ndugu na dada zetu kujenga uhusiano huohuo katika maisha yao wenyewe. Sababu ya sisi kuwa na matumaini si kwamba watu ni wema ajabu—hatuhitaji kuishi muda mrefu sana kutambua kwamba sivyo walivyo. Sababu ya kuwa na matumaini ni kwamba tunamtumikia Mungu wa ajabu na mwaminifu anayetembea pamoja nasi katika majaribu yetu mabaya zaidi.

Kumbuka kwamba Tuna Matumaini Tusiyostahili

Ujumbe wa Yesu kuhusu msamaha unaweka wazi kwamba moja ya sababu kuu za kuwasamehe wengine katika maisha yetu ni kwamba tumepokea msamaha mkubwa ambao hatukustahili. Ndivyo ilivyo pia kuhusu matumaini.

Kila mmoja wetu hakuwa na matumaini wala sababu ya kutarajia kupokea matumaini, lakini bado tulipewa mwanga katika giza letu. Huenda sehemu ya sababu ya sisi kupata shida sana kutarajia mambo mema kwa watu wanaotuzunguka ni kwamba hatukumbuki jinsi tulivyokuwa bila matumaini kabla hatujapata neema.

Ikiwa Yesu aliweza kuleta matumaini katika maisha yetu yasiyokuwa na matumaini, basi kwa hakika anaweza kufanya mambo ya ajabu katika mioyo na maisha ya wengine wanaotuzunguka. Watu pekee ambao tunapaswa kukata tamaa kuwahusu ni wale ambao Mwokozi wetu pia amekata tamaa kuwahusu.

Juhudi Ndogo Huleta Mabadiliko Kweli

Nakumbuka mazungumzo na kijana aliyekuwa akipanga kuingia katika taaluma ya udaktari na aliyekuwa na mpango wa kwenda katika nchi ya kigeni kuwahudumia watu huko. Tulipokuwa tukizungumza, mwanamume mwenye umri mkubwa alijiunga na mazungumzo na kueleza kwamba aliona matumaini machache ya mabadiliko katika nchi zinazoendelea.

Watu katika nchi hizo hawakuwa na nia ya kuboresha afya zao na hawakufanya hata kiwango cha chini kilichohitajika kuzuia mambo kama minyoo na vimelea. Madaktari na wauguzi hawangeweza kuleta mabadiliko katika mazingira kama hayo.

Niliweza kuhisi moyo wa kijana huyo ukivunjika mtu huyu mwenye umri mkubwa alipokuwa akizungumza. Alikuwa na uzoefu, naye alikuwa amekata tamaa. Jambo la kusikitisha ni kwamba pia alikuwa akipora matumaini ya mtu ambaye bado alikuwa na hamu ya kutumikia.

Nilipokuwa katika mafunzo, daktari wa upasuaji aliniambia kwamba madaktari wa familia hawakufanya chochote hasa. Waliwaweka tu wagonjwa wao hai mpaka walipokuja tena ofisini, ilhali madaktari wa upasuaji kweli “waliwatengeneza” watu—kwa kuondoa sehemu ya mwili iliyokuwa ikisababisha tatizo.

Mwishowe, juhudi ndogo huleta mabadiliko kweli. Sifanyi upasuaji wa ubongo, lakini bado ninaweza kuleta mabadiliko katika maisha ya mtu mwingine—huenda kwa kutumia tu muda kidogo kumsikiliza na kuomba. Hili ni kweli kwetu sote.

Zaidi ya hayo, tunatambua kwamba kufanya juhudi hizi hubadilisha maisha yetu wenyewe kuwa bora. Yesu aliwaambia kondoo kwamba walipowahudumia “walio wadogo zaidi miongoni mwa hawa ndugu zangu,” walikuwa wakimhudumia Yeye.

Hata ikiwa maisha ya mtu yeyote hayaboreshwi, Mwokozi wetu anajua matamanio yetu na anahisi juhudi zetu, naye atazithawabisha siku moja.

Mambo Machache ya Kukumbuka

Tunapokabiliwa na kushindwa, tunaelekea kwenda katika mojawapo ya mielekeo miwili. Sisi wenye mtazamo wa matumaini huelekea kuamini kwamba tukio hili lilikuwa la pekee na kwamba wakati ujao bado una mwanga. Kwa upande mwingine, wenye mtazamo wa kukata tamaa wanaamini kwamba kushindwa ni kwa kudumu, kunawahusu wao binafsi, na kunaenea katika kila sehemu ya maisha.

Wenye mtazamo wa kukata tamaa wanaamini kwamba kushindwa kwao kunatokana na kasoro za kiasili katika tabia zao, na kwamba mambo haya yanaathiri maisha yao yote na huenda yasibadilike. Tofauti na mtu mwenye haki anayeanguka ili ainuke tena, watu hawa huanguka na kubaki pale wanapoangukia, wakiwa wameshindwa tangu mwanzo.

Tunaposhughulika na watu wengine, tunahitaji kuwapa neema ileile tunayopaswa kujipa wenyewe. Wao pia wanakua, na wakishindwa leo, watafanya vizuri zaidi kesho. Huenda wakashindwa tena, lakini angalau “watashindwa kwa namna iliyo bora zaidi.”

Hitimisho

Mtazamo wa kutarajia mabaya umeenea sana katika ulimwengu wetu. Wengi wamekata tamaa ya kuwa na wakati ujao ulio bora, na hilo linaeleweka kwa wale walioweka matumaini yao katika taasisi za ulimwengu huu. Hakuna matumaini ya kweli katika serikali, katika majeshi, wala katika urasimu.

Wimbo unasema, “Ee, kutokuwa na tumaini katika Yesu, ulimwengu huu lazima uwe na giza kubwa namna gani!” Kwa maana Yesu ndiye anayeleta mwanga katika giza letu na kutuwezesha kuendelea, hata wengine wanapotuangusha.

Mungu ndiye anayetukomboa. Yeye ndiye aliyewatuma manabii, ingawa ujumbe wao ulipuuzwa na manabii wakateswa. Yeye ndiye anayeendelea kuwa na matumaini kwa ajili yetu, hata tulipomwangusha mara nyingi sana hapo zamani.

Yeye ndiye sababu ya sisi kuendelea. Yeye ndiye sababu ya sisi kuwa na matumaini, si kwa ajili yetu wenyewe tu, bali pia kwa ajili ya ndugu zetu.

Eight-year-old Jamin wasn’t very smart. Or at least that’s what his older brother told him. Almost daily, brother Kenny found ways to remind Jamin of his shortcomings and laugh at his blunders.

“Jamin, you will never be smart”, Kenny said. Deep inside Jamin felt resigned to a life of muddled trip-ups. Would he always be clumsy? Would he always say things wrong? That’s what Kenny said.

Jamin believed Kenny’s lectures with wide-eyed belief. Kenny was three years older than him, so he must be right. Very well, then Jamin would be simple. Kenny would be smart. Life was not fair. Dad and Mom disliked Kenny’s proud talk and punished him whenever they walked in on one of his speeches. But Kenny had a way of avoiding earshot. So he continued mocking Jamin.

Grandma Otto watched these trials from her rocker on the porch. She was a quiet old lady.

“Jamin, do you know where Kenny is?” Mom asked with a smile. “It’s almost supper time.”

“He went to check his coyote traps. I’ll go find him.”

There was a chill in the air as he tramped up over the lawn, and the sun was growing old as he crossed the border of the woods. The fleeting shadows scurried over the hills. The chill deepened as he stumped further in. He breathed the rich air and followed Kenny’s trail. Eventually, the trail would end up in a meadow, but Jamin hoped he would find Kenny before he had to go that far. The various traps had been checked already, so Jamin knew Kenny had come this way. Jamin trudged on resolutely. His golden head caught the tired beams that fled from the sun as they flickered through the trees. And soon those too had faded leaving behind the musky smell of the woods. The fall webworms had been at work, and their web curtains shuttered from branches overhead.

At length, as the trees subdued and thinned, and the meadow appeared Jamin knew this was the end of his brother’s trap route. If Kenny wasn’t here, he wouldn’t know where else to look.

But Kenny was there. As Jamin clumped into the meadow, he could see a frustrated heap to his right. The heap’s voice had a familiar ring. The heap’s face was lit in pain. The heap was Kenny. “Are you alright? What happened?” Jamin felt strange, seeing Kenny scrunched in the dirt. Kenny was smart. “Did you step in a trap?”

“Yes, Jamin. I..I wasn’t looking where I was going. Help me. Please.”

Jamin bent and found an ankle firmly held in the jaws of a steel trap. Darkness stained the ground around Kenny. Quickly, Jamin’s strong arms pried open the jaws. Kenny reeled free. “Can you walk?”

“Yes. I think so. If you support me, I can hobble along.”

“Dad and Mom will be worried. We’ve missed supper.”

Sure enough, as the brothers hobbled back through the woods, they heard the long calling of their father. Jamin called back, and he was by their side in a moment, seeing the ankle and scooping up Kenny like a hurt sheep. The odd little band hurried home, and the screen door banged shut as Dad swept across the porch. Jamin went to the wash house and scrubbed his hands. He headed for the front door.

“Jamin.” It was Grandma. The porch light showed her in her old rocker. A heavy comforter lay on her shoulders.

“Yes, Grandma?”

“Do you think you are not very smart?”

“That’s what Kenny says.” Jamin squirmed.

“You were strong enough to open the trap, and Kenny wasn’t. You were brave enough to find him in the dark. Lots of young boys wouldn’t be.” Jamin was silent. Grandma Otto rocked some more, then smiled. “God made you the way you are for a reason, Jamin. He made Kenny the way he is for a reason. He has a plan for you, and a place only you can fill, you know.”

Jamin turned and walked into the warm kitchen. He was smiling.

Jamin mwenye umri wa miaka minane hakuwa mwerevu sana. Au angalau hivyo ndivyo kaka yake alivyomwambia. Karibu kila siku, kaka yake Kenny alipata njia za kumkumbusha Jamin mapungufu yake na kucheka makosa yake.

“Jamin, hutakuwa mwerevu kamwe,” Kenny alisema. Moyoni mwake, Jamin alihisi amekubali kwamba maisha yake yangekuwa ya kuchanganyikiwa na kufanya makosa. Je, angeendelea kuwa mtu asiye na ustadi daima? Je, angeendelea kusema mambo vibaya daima? Hivyo ndivyo Kenny alivyosema.

Jamin aliamini mahubiri ya Kenny kwa imani isiyo na shaka. Kenny alikuwa mkubwa kuliko yeye kwa miaka mitatu, kwa hiyo lazima alikuwa sahihi. Basi, sawa, Jamin angekuwa mtu asiye na akili nyingi. Kenny angekuwa mwerevu. Maisha hayakuwa ya haki. Baba na Mama hawakupenda maneno ya majivuno ya Kenny na walimwadhibu kila walipomkuta akitoa mojawapo ya hotuba zake. Lakini Kenny alikuwa na namna ya kusema bila wao kusikia. Kwa hiyo aliendelea kumdhihaki Jamin.

Bibi Otto alitazama majaribu haya akiwa kwenye kiti chake cha kubembea barazani. Alikuwa mwanamke mzee mtulivu.

“Jamin, unajua Kenny yuko wapi?” Mama aliuliza huku akitabasamu. “Karibu ni wakati wa chakula cha jioni.”

“Ameenda kukagua mitego yake ya koyoti. Nitaenda kumtafuta.”

Hewa ilikuwa na ubaridi alipokuwa akipanda kupitia kwenye nyasi za uani, na jua lilikuwa likielekea kutua alipovuka mpaka wa msitu. Vivuli vya muda mfupi vilikimbia juu ya vilima. Ubaridi ulizidi alipoingia ndani zaidi kwa hatua nzito. Alivuta hewa yenye harufu nzito na kufuata njia ya Kenny. Hatimaye, njia hiyo ingefika kwenye uwanda wa nyasi, lakini Jamin alitumaini angempata Kenny kabla hajalazimika kwenda mbali kiasi hicho. Mitego mbalimbali ilikuwa tayari imekaguliwa, kwa hiyo Jamin alijua Kenny alikuwa amepitia huko. Jamin aliendelea kutembea kwa hatua nzito, akiwa na azimio thabiti. Nywele zake za rangi ya dhahabu zilipokea miale hafifu iliyotoka kwenye jua na kupenya katikati ya miti. Na punde miale hiyo nayo ikafifia, ikiacha harufu nzito ya msitu. Viwavi wanaosuka utando wakati wa vuli walikuwa wamefanya kazi yao, na mapazia yao ya utando yalining’inia kama vifuniko kwenye matawi yaliyokuwa juu yake.

Hatimaye, miti ilipopungua na kutawanyika, na uwanda wa nyasi ukaonekana, Jamin alijua hapa ndipo njia ya mitego ya kaka yake ilipoishia. Ikiwa Kenny hakuwa hapa, asingejua mahali pengine pa kumtafuta.

Lakini Kenny alikuwa hapo. Jamin alipoingia kwenye uwanda kwa hatua nzito, aliweza kuona mtu aliyejikunyata kwa kufadhaika upande wake wa kulia. Sauti ya huyo aliyejikunyata ilikuwa ya kufahamika. Uso wake ulionyesha maumivu. Huyo aliyejikunyata alikuwa Kenny. “Uko salama? Kumetokea nini?” Jamin alihisi jambo lisilo la kawaida alipomwona Kenny amejikunyata chini kwenye udongo. Kenny alikuwa mwerevu. “Ulikanyaga mtego?”

“Ndiyo, Jamin. Mi..mimi sikuwa nikiangalia nilikokuwa nikienda. Nisaidie. Tafadhali.”

Jamin aliinama na kuona kifundo cha mguu kimeshikwa kwa nguvu na taya za mtego wa chuma cha pua. Giza lilitanda juu ya ardhi iliyomzunguka Kenny. Kwa haraka, Jamin alitumia mikono yake yenye nguvu kufungua taya hizo. Kenny aliyumba alipojinasua. “Unaweza kutembea?”

“Ndiyo. Nafikiri naweza. Ukinishikilia, naweza kwenda nikichechemea.”

“Baba na Mama watakuwa na wasiwasi. Tumekosa chakula cha jioni.”

Kwa kweli, ndugu hao walipokuwa wakirudi kupitia msituni kwa kuchechemea, walimsikia baba yao akiita kwa sauti ndefu. Jamin aliitikia, na baada ya muda mfupi baba alikuwa pembeni yao; alikiona kifundo cha mguu na kumwinua Kenny kama kondoo aliyejeruhiwa. Kikundi hicho kidogo kisicho cha kawaida kiliharakisha kurudi nyumbani, na mlango wa wavu ukafungwa kwa kishindo Baba alipovuka baraza kwa haraka. Jamin alienda kwenye kibanda cha kuogea na kusugua mikono yake mpaka ikawa safi. Akaelekea kwenye mlango wa mbele.

“Jamin.” Alikuwa Bibi. Mwanga wa barazani ulimwonyesha akiwa kwenye kiti chake cha zamani cha kubembea. Blanketi zito lilikuwa limetanda mabegani mwake.

“Naam, Bibi?”

“Unafikiri wewe si mwerevu sana?”

“Hivyo ndivyo Kenny anavyosema.” Jamin alijitikisa kwa kutokuwa na raha.

“Ulikuwa na nguvu za kutosha kufungua mtego, lakini Kenny hakuwa nazo. Ulikuwa na ujasiri wa kutosha kumtafuta gizani. Wavulana wengi wadogo wasingekuwa nao.” Jamin alinyamaza. Bibi Otto aliendelea kubembea kidogo, kisha akatabasamu. “Mungu alikuumba jinsi ulivyo kwa sababu fulani, Jamin. Alimuumba Kenny jinsi alivyo kwa sababu fulani. Ana mpango kwa ajili yako, na nafasi ambayo wewe peke yako unaweza kuijaza, unajua.”

Jamin aligeuka na kuingia jikoni kulikokuwa na joto. Alikuwa akitabasamu.
